topics.title: 1. Language Translators, Generations & Programming Basics
topics.theory:
- **Language generations:** 1GL = **machine language** (binary, first-generation computers), 2GL = **assembly** (mnemonics, machine-dependent), 3GL = high-level (C, Java, Pascal), 4GL = SQL-style, 5GL = AI/logic.
- **Translators:** **Assembler** = assembly -> machine code; **Compiler** = whole high-level program -> object/machine code at once; **Interpreter** = translates and runs line by line (Perl, Python, JavaScript are typically interpreted; C is compiled).
- **Build pipeline (C):** preprocessor (`#include`, `#define`, macro expansion) -> compiler -> assembler -> **object file** (input to linker) -> **linker** -> **executable (.exe)** -> loader puts it in memory.
- **Compiler phases:** lexical analysis (tokens) -> syntax analysis (parse tree) -> **semantic analysis** (type checking, symbol table) -> intermediate code -> optimisation -> code generation.
- **Errors:** **syntax** error = language rules violated (caught at compile time); **logical** error = wrong output, no crash; **run-time** error = fails during execution.
- **High-level language features:** portability, easier debugging, machine independence; assembly is machine-dependent. A good language offers clarity, simplicity, abstraction and ease of verification.
- **JIT (Just-In-Time) compiling** converts intermediate language (Java bytecode / .NET IL) to native code at run time; .NET compiles to **CIL/MSIL**, a CPU-independent instruction set.
- **Firsts:** FORTRAN = **Formula Translation** (scientific); C++ by **Bjarne Stroustrup**; C by Dennis Ritchie; Pascal by Niklaus Wirth.
- **Front-end tech:** HTML, CSS, JavaScript; PL/SQL is back-end (database server side).
- **Sandboxing** = running untrusted code in an isolated, controlled environment; **user documentation** explains purpose, usage and output, not internal code formatting.

qs.stem: _________ is a system software package that converts a high level language program to machine language.
qs.sol: A Compiler is a translator used to convert high-level programming language code (Source Code) into machine language (Object Code) all at once. This allows the computer's processor to understand and execute the instructions.
qs.rel: Translator types: compiler (whole program), interpreter (line by line), assembler (assembly to machine). Neighbours: the linker joins object files, the loader places the executable in memory, a debugger finds errors.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a front-end technology?
qs.sol: Front-end technologies like JavaScript, HTML, and CSS handle user interfaces directly. PL/SQL is a backend database language used for server-side operations, making it the exception here.
qs.rel: Front-end = browser side (HTML structure, CSS style, JavaScript behaviour). Back-end/server technologies include PL/SQL, PHP, ASP, Java servlets. Examiner may ask which is a database language or server-side scripting.

qs.stem: _____ converts a source code to object code.
qs.sol: A compiler translates high-level source code into low-level object code that a computer can execute. This differs from interpreters which run code line-by-line or linkers which combine object files.
qs.rel: Compiler converts the entire source into object code and lists errors afterwards; interpreter translates and runs line by line. Related: object code goes to the linker, which produces the executable; loader runs it.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is the feature(s) of High level programming languages?
 I. Portability
 II. Easy debugging
qs.sol:
English Explanation:

High-level programming languages are designed to make programming easier, more understandable, and less dependent on hardware.

Statement I: Portability

This statement is correct because high-level languages are portable. A program written in a high-level language can run on different systems with little or no modification after compilation.

Statement II: Easy debugging

This statement is also correct because high-level languages use readable syntax similar to human language, making errors easier to identify and debug.

Since both statements are correct, the correct answer is Both I and II.
qs.rel: High-level languages offer portability, machine independence and easier debugging. Related: assembly is machine-dependent; machine language is binary, the only language the CPU runs directly; HLLs need translation.

qs.stem: The programming language C++ was developed by:
qs.sol: C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs as an extension of the C language with object-oriented features. Blaise Pascal is associated with Pascal, Dennis Ritchie with C, and Alan Turing with theoretical computer science.
qs.rel: C++ was created by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs (originally 'C with Classes'). Neighbours: C by Dennis Ritchie, Java by James Gosling, Pascal by Niklaus Wirth, Python by Guido van Rossum.

qs.stem:
The programming of first generation computers was done in ____ language.
 I. Machine
 II. High level
qs.sol:
First generation computers used machine language for programming. Machine language consists of binary digits (0s and 1s) that are directly understood by the computer hardware.

High-level languages were developed later to make programming easier and more user-friendly. Therefore, first generation computers did not use high-level languages.

Hence:

Statement I is correct.

Statement II is incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is Only I.
qs.rel: First generation = vacuum-tube machines programmed in binary machine language. Related: second generation used assembly, third high-level languages; each generation of languages (1GL..5GL) differs from hardware generations.

qs.stem: Which translator is used to convert assembly language to machine language?
qs.sol: An assembler converts assembly language programs into machine language.
qs.rel: Assembler turns assembly mnemonics into machine code, mostly one-to-one. Related: assembly is machine-dependent; macros expand in an assembler pass; a compiler maps one high-level statement to many instructions.

qs.stem: When the rules of the programming language are not followed it gives ____ errors.
qs.sol:
Every programming language has a set of grammatical rules called syntax.
If a programmer writes code that violates these rules, the compiler/interpreter generates a syntax error.

Example:

printf("Hello")

Missing semicolon (;) causes a syntax error in C language.
qs.rel: Violating language grammar gives a syntax error at compile time. Related: logical errors give wrong output with no message; run-time errors (division by zero) occur during execution; semantic errors involve type misuse.

qs.stem: What is the full form of FORTRAN computer programming language?
qs.sol:
FORTRAN is one of the earliest high-level programming languages developed mainly for scientific and engineering calculations. The word FORTRAN is derived from:

FORmula TRANslation

Hence, the full form of FORTRAN is Formula Translation.
qs.rel: FORTRAN = Formula Translation, an early scientific language (1950s). Related: COBOL for business, LISP for AI, ALGOL for algorithms, BASIC for beginners, Pascal for teaching.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT an attribute of good programming languages?
qs.sol:
A good programming language should have features like:

Clarity, simplicity, and unity → makes programs easy to understand.

Support for abstraction → helps manage complexity.

Ease of program verification → helps detect and reduce errors.

Portability is desirable so programs can run on different systems.

Non portability is not an attribute of a good programming language because it limits the use of programs across platforms.
qs.rel: Good language traits: clarity, simplicity, unity, abstraction support, ease of verification, portability. Non-portability is a drawback. Related: orthogonality, readability, writability.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is a typically interpreted language?
 I. C
 II. Perl
qs.sol:
An interpreted language is a programming language in which the code is executed line by line by an interpreter, without requiring complete compilation beforehand.

C is generally a compiled programming language. A C program is converted into machine code using a compiler before execution.

Perl is commonly considered an interpreted language because Perl scripts are usually executed by the Perl interpreter.

Therefore, only statement II is correct.
qs.rel: Perl is typically interpreted; C is compiled. Related: Python, JavaScript, Ruby, PHP are interpreted/scripting; Java is compiled to bytecode then interpreted/JIT-compiled.

qs.stem: When does the .exe file is created in C language?
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: The official paper cancelled the item because compilation may name the whole build process. The executable is emitted after the linker combines object code and libraries.
qs.rel: The .exe is produced after linking object files. Related: compilation yields object (.o/.obj) files; the linker resolves library calls; preprocess -> compile -> assemble -> link.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct regarding Assembly language?
I. An assembler converts (or assembles) the symbolic program of an Assembly language into its equivalent machine program.
II. A program written in an assembly language is machine dependent.
qs.sol: An assembler translates assembly-language symbolic code into machine code, and assembly-language programs are machine dependent.
qs.rel: Assembler converts symbolic assembly into machine code; assembly is machine-dependent. Related: uses mnemonics and labels; one-to-one with instructions; faster but less portable than HLL.

qs.sol: Sandboxing provides a controlled execution environment for extracted or untrusted programs. It isolates the code to prevent potential damage to the host system. Other security concepts like spoofing or honeypots do not serve this specific isolation purpose.
qs.rel: Sandboxing runs untrusted code in an isolated environment. Related: Java applet sandbox, browser tabs, containers/VMs; a security manager restricts file and network access.

qs.stem:
The process of compiling Intermediate Language programs to the actual machine language on the target platform prior to execution is known as ______.

I.  Just-In-Time compiling

II.  First-In-Time compiling
qs.sol:
Concept

Intermediate language is a portable representation of a program. A runtime may interpret its instructions or compile them into native machine instructions for the target processor. Compilation models differ by timing: ahead-of-time compilation produces native code before the application runs; just-in-time compilation produces it on demand during application runtime, immediately before a method or block of native code is used.

Application

The stem asks for a name for translating Intermediate Language to machine code on the target platform before execution. …
qs.rel: JIT compiling converts intermediate language to native code at run time. Related: JVM bytecode and .NET CIL are examples; AOT compiles ahead; interpreters execute without translating.

qs.stem: ________ is a sequence of bytes organised into blocks that is understood by system's linker.
qs.sol: The correct answer is Object files. These are sequences of bytes organized into blocks or sections containing machine code and symbols required for the linker to combine multiple modules. Unlike source files which are human-readable or executables processed by loaders, object files specifically target the linking stage.
qs.rel: An object file holds machine code in sections for the linker. Related: source -> object -> executable; relocatable code; libraries are archives of object files.

qs.stem:
Which of the following are included in the user documentation of program?
 I. Program formatting
 II. Description of program and its purpose
 III. Description of program output
qs.sol: User documentation is designed for end-users to understand how to operate the software effectively. Program formatting refers to internal code structure and belongs in technical documentation for developers. Describing the program's purpose and output provides necessary context for users interacting with the system daily. Therefore, items II and III are appropriate inclusions for user documentation while excluding internal formatting details.
qs.rel: User documentation covers the program's purpose, inputs, outputs and use; formatting belongs to internal documentation. Related: technical, system and maintenance docs.

qs.stem: _____ is a CPU independent machine language style instruction set into which .NET Framework programs are compiled.
qs.sol: The .NET Framework compiles source code into an intermediate language called Intermediate Language (IL) or Common Intermediate Language (CIL). This instruction set is CPU independent and executed by the runtime environment.
qs.rel: IL (CIL/MSIL) is the CPU-independent instruction set .NET compiles to. Related: JIT converts IL to native; Java equivalent is bytecode; assemblies hold IL.

qs.stem: Which of the following phase of the compiler, gathers type information and saves it in either the syntax tree or the symbol table, for subsequent use during intermediate code generation?
qs.sol: Concept: In the classical compiler pipeline, the front end has three distinct phases: lexical analysis (produces tokens), syntax analysis (uses those tokens to build a parse tree/AST reflecting only grammatical structure), and semantic analysis (checks static semantics -- most importantly type compatibility -- and attaches the derived type information onto the syntax tree's nodes or into the symbol table). Only after this annotation is the tree "type-complete" and ready for the back end (intermediate code generation, optimization, code generation) to consume. …
qs.rel: Semantic analysis performs type checking and fills the symbol table. Related: lexical analysis makes tokens, syntax analysis builds parse tree, then intermediate code, optimisation, code generation.

qs.sol: The subquery produces an empty set. The predicate ProductID IN (empty set) is false for every Product row, so the DELETE affects zero rows and leaves both tables unchanged.
qs.rel: IN with an empty subquery matches nothing, so DELETE removes zero rows. Related: NOT IN empty is true for all; NULLs in NOT IN produce unknown; DELETE without WHERE removes all rows.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about pre-processor in C/C++?
 I. To replace each #include directive with the contents of the designated file.
 II. To replace each escape sequence with designated character.
 III. To process macro definitions and expand macro calls.
qs.sol:
Concept:
The C/C++ build pipeline runs distinct translation phases: the preprocessor performs purely textual, directive-level substitution — expanding #include and #define — before the compiler ever runs. Interpreting the meaning of tokens already in the source, such as converting an escape sequence into its character value, belongs to the compiler's lexical-analysis phase, not the preprocessor.

Application:

Statement I — #include is replaced with the contents of the designated file: this is exactly the preprocessor's textual substitution job — True. …
qs.rel: Preprocessor replaces #include with file contents and expands macros; it does not process escape sequences or type-check. Related: #define, #ifdef, #pragma; compile follows.

qs.sol: The `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` statement creates a new table and populates it with the rows returned by the query. Selecting all columns and rows from `ProductOrder` gives `CREATE TABLE ProductOrder_2026 AS SELECT * FROM ProductOrder;`
qs.rel: CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies structure and chosen rows into a new table (constraints not copied). Related: SELECT INTO in SQL Server; INSERT ... SELECT; views.

qs.stem:
Which of the given options best describes the truthfulness of the following statements?
 i) Assembly languages are machine dependent.
 ii) A compiler is a program which produces a machine level program from the specifications of a high-level language.
 iii) An interpreter translates and executes each program statement, one at a time.
 iv) ‘BASIC’ language is an interactive programming language.
qs.sol:
Correct Answer: Option 1: i-True, ii-True, iii-True, iv-True

Statement i: Assembly languages are machine dependent.

True: Assembly language uses mnemonics that correspond directly to a specific CPU's architecture and instruction set. Therefore, code written for one type of processor will not work on another.

Statement ii: A compiler is a program which produces a machine level program from the specifications of a high-level language.

True: As seen in previous examples, a compiler translates the entire source code of a high-level language into a machine-readable object file (executable) at once.

Statement iii: An interpreter translates and executes each program statement, one at a time. …
qs.rel: Assembly is machine-dependent; a compiler outputs machine-level code; assemblers translate assembly. Related: interpreter executes directly; linker/loader roles; high-level portability.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not an example of a Programming Language?
qs.sol: C++, Python, and Ruby are widely recognized as high-level programming languages. In contrast, Impress is a presentation program included in office suites like LibreOffice, not a coding language. Therefore, Impress is the option that is not an example of a programming language.

COBOL, BASIC, FORTRAN, C, C++, and Java use abstractions such as variables, statements, and functions.

ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange. It is a character encoding standard used to represent text in computers and other devices. ASCII uses 7 bits to represent 128 possible characters, including letters, digits, punctuation, and control characters.

qs.stem: C was primarily developed as a
qs.sol:
Concept: A class defines a type with state and behavior; an object is a concrete instance of that type. A reference provides a way to refer to an existing instance.

The instance and the variable used to refer to it are distinct concepts: the instance carries state, while a reference variable supplies access to it.

Application: Consider a C++ class Person with an age field.

Person instance;
Person& ref = instance;

The declaration Person instance creates an instance of the class Person; that instance is an object.

The declaration Person& ref = instance binds ref to the existing instance. The ampersand in this declaration specifies a reference. …

The C programming language was originally developed at Bell Labs by Dennis Ritchie for system programming, especially for developing the UNIX operating system.
 Hence, its primary purpose was system-level programming.

qs.sol:
Concept

JDBC separates opening a database session from executing SQL. A connection-producing component selects a registered driver and returns a Connection; statement and result objects operate later in that workflow.

Application

The application calls DriverManager.getConnection(url, ...) with a JDBC URL and connection properties.

DriverManager searches the registered JDBC drivers for one that accepts the URL.

The selected driver opens the database session, and the call returns a Connection object to the application.

Cross-check and contrast

qs.stem: Component(s) of interpreter is/are :
qs.sol:
An interpreter is a type of language processor that executes source code instructions directly, line by line, without compiling the entire program into machine code beforehand.

To execute high-level program logic on the fly, a standard interpreter framework integrates several core components:

Symbol Table: Tracks all declared entities (variables, methods, classes) along with their data types, scopes, and memory locations. It is dynamically accessed and updated during runtime.

Data Store: Refers to the runtime memory layout (including call stacks, heaps, and value registers) used to physically hold the application's runtime data. …

Bottom-up parsing builds the parse tree from leaves to root by repeatedly shifting input symbols and reducing them to non-terminals.
⇒ Hence, it is called Shift-Reduce Parsing

Answer:  Non-portable (गैर-पोर्टेबल) is not a valid feature of Java.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not a primitive data type?
qs.sol:
Concept

Java divides every type into exactly two families. A primitive type is one of the eight types built into the language itself: the variable stores the value directly in its own memory slot, the type name is a lowercase reserved keyword, the variable can never be null, and the value has no methods.

Every other type - a class, an interface or an array - is a reference type. Such a variable does not store the object; it stores a reference to an object that lives on the heap, its default value is null, and the object it points to can expose methods. …

The structure or format of data is called Syntax. In data communication, syntax refers to the arrangement of data blocks, specifying how data is presented or read (e.g., the first 8 bits represent the sender's address).

Note: According to standard networking textbooks (like Forouzan), Syntax is the correct definitions for data format.

Correct Answer: Syntax (Option A).

qs.stem: Which method of program translation in a computer produces an executable file that can be run independently on the system?
qs.sol:
Program translators convert source code into a form the CPU can execute. They differ in WHEN that translation happens and WHETHER the translated output survives as an independent file, separate from both the translator program and the original source.

Here, a compiler translates the entire high-level source program before execution, producing a machine-code executable file (directly, or after linking any generated object code). Once that file exists, it runs standalone -- the compiler and the original source code are no longer needed at run time. …
Linking resolves external functions and libraries after compilation. An unresolved symbol can therefore occur even when syntax compilation succeeds.

qs.stem: Which statement indicates an action to be performed during execution of assembled program?
qs.sol:
During the execution of an assembled program, the processor performs specific actions based on instructions.

Imperative statements explicitly define commands that the processor executes sequentially to manipulate data and control flow.

Declarative statements describe relationships or data states rather than specific execution steps, making them unsuitable for this context.

qs.stem:
Which of the following flowcharts is most appropriate for printing the first 8 multiples of 9?

A
B
C
D
qs.sol:
Concept: Every counted loop is defined by four parts — an initial value, a continuation test, a body, and an update. Which values such a loop emits is fixed by three independent choices: where the counter starts, whether the test boundary is inclusive (I ≤ limit) or exclusive (I < limit), and whether the update runs before or after the output step. Change any one of them and the emitted list changes, even though every box on its own still looks arithmetically fine.

Application: The target is exactly eight numbers — 9 × 1 up to 9 × 8, that is 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72. …

topics.deep:
- **Generations of languages:** 1GL machine code (binary 0/1, first-generation computers, hardware-specific, fastest, hardest); 2GL assembly (mnemonics like `ADD`, `MOV`, one-to-one with machine instructions, **machine-dependent**); 3GL high-level (C, C++, Java, Pascal, FORTRAN, COBOL - portable, English-like); 4GL (SQL, report generators); 5GL (Prolog, constraint/AI languages).
- **Translators compared:**

| Translator | Input -> Output | Unit of translation | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Assembler | assembly -> machine code | whole program | one-to-one mapping |
| Compiler | high-level -> object/machine code | whole program | errors listed after full scan; fast run time |
| Interpreter | high-level -> executes | line by line | slower run, stops at first error (Perl, Python, JavaScript, BASIC) |
| Preprocessor | source -> expanded source | text | `#include`, `#define`, conditional compile |
| Linker | object files + libraries -> executable | files | resolves external references |
| Loader | executable -> memory | - | allocates memory, starts execution |

- **C build pipeline:** `.c` -> preprocessor -> compiler -> `.s` -> assembler -> `.o` (**object file**, sequence of bytes in sections that the *linker* understands) -> **linker** -> `.exe`/`a.out` -> loader. The **.exe is produced after linking**, not after compilation.
- **Compiler phases (front end):** lexical analysis (source -> tokens), syntax analysis (tokens -> parse tree, grammar check), **semantic analysis** (type checking; stores type info in syntax tree/**symbol table**), then intermediate code generation, optimisation, target code generation (back end). Symbol table and error handler are used by all phases.
- **Error kinds:** syntax (rule violation, e.g. missing `;`) - compile time; semantic (type mismatch); logical (wrong result); run-time (divide by zero, array bound). Debugging = locating and removing errors.
- **Java/.NET:** `javac` -> **bytecode** -> JVM interprets or **JIT**-compiles to native code. .NET languages -> **CIL/MSIL** -> CLR JIT. JIT = Just-In-Time (not "First-In-Time").
- **Features of good languages:** clarity, simplicity, unity, support for abstraction, ease of program verification, portability, reasonable cost of translation/execution.
- **Historic facts:** FORTRAN (1957, Formula Translation, John Backus/IBM, scientific); COBOL (business); BASIC; Pascal (Wirth, 1970); C (Ritchie, 1972, Bell Labs); C++ (Stroustrup, 1979-85, Bell Labs); Java (James Gosling, Sun, 1995); Simula (first OOP, 1967).
- **Documentation:** *user documentation* = purpose of the program, how to run it, description of inputs and outputs; *internal documentation* = comments, formatting, naming; *technical documentation* = design, algorithms.
- **Sandbox:** isolated environment (Java applet sandbox, browser, VM) limiting file/network/system access for untrusted code.
- **Other small facts:** front-end = what runs in the browser (HTML structure, CSS style, JavaScript behaviour); back-end = server, database, PL/SQL, PHP. `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (empty subquery)` removes 0 rows; `CREATE TABLE t2 AS SELECT * FROM t1` copies structure and rows.
- **Common traps:** compile does not produce `.exe` by itself; interpreter is not "faster"; assembly is not portable; a compiler reports errors for the entire program, an interpreter stops at the first.
- **Likely question angles:**
  - Which translator converts X to Y (assembler/compiler/interpreter/linker/loader/preprocessor)?
  - Which compiler phase generates tokens / builds the parse tree / does type checking / produces optimised code?
  - Which output does `javac` produce, and what does `javap` or `java` do?
  - Stage at which an executable is created in C; what a linker resolves.
  - Match languages with their creators or purposes (FORTRAN, COBOL, Pascal, Simula, Ada).
  - Interpreted vs compiled: classify C, Perl, Python, Java, JavaScript.
  - Machine vs assembly vs high-level: statement true/false (portability, speed, debugging).
  - Identify syntax vs logical vs run-time error given a scenario.
  - What does JIT do; what is CIL/MSIL?

topics.title: 2. Modular & Event-Driven Programming
topics.theory:
- **Modular programming** divides a problem into independent **modules** (functions, subroutines, macros); benefits: **reusability, easier testing/debugging, maintainability, ease of use**. C++ (headers, namespaces) and Java (packages, classes) support it.
- Data passed between modules are **parameters**; modules interact through an **interface**; grouping code into a reusable unit = **modularisation**.
- **Subprograms:** functions (return a value) and subroutines/procedures (usually do not).
- **Top-down design:** analyse problem -> write main module -> write remaining modules -> connect modules in order -> revise and resequence.
- **Event-driven programming:** flow of control is determined by **external events** (clicks, key presses, messages), not a fixed sequence; the model is **asynchronous**.
- **Event** = a piece of data/signal sent by a producer and consumed by a consumer; **event handler** = a **callback routine** run asynchronously on the event; **event listener** waits for the event.
- **Event loop** continuously (1) detects events and (2) dispatches them to handlers; the **event queue** orders events for processing.
- Components talk indirectly through an intermediary (**message queue / broker**); an event failing after retries goes to a **dead letter queue**.
- **Event splitting** = one incoming event handled by multiple entities; contrast with event merging/combining.
- Object-oriented model is **bottom-up**; procedural/structured approach is **top-down**.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is/are advantages of modular programming? 

(i) Easier to test 
(ii) Reusability
qs.sol: Modular programming separates functionality into independent modules. This structure makes individual components easier to test in isolation, validating statement (i). Additionally, well-defined modules can be reused across different projects or within the same system, confirming statement (ii). Both listed benefits are standard advantages of this approach.
qs.rel: Modular design splits a program into independent units that can be tested separately. Other benefits: reuse, easier maintenance, parallel team work. Related: cohesion should be high, coupling low.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is/are modular programming languages? 

(i) C++ 
(ii) Java
qs.sol: Modular programming involves breaking code into separate sections. C++ supports this via header files and namespaces, while Java uses packages and classes. Since both languages offer these features for code organization, they are considered modular programming languages.
qs.rel: Modular support: C++ uses header files, namespaces and classes; Java uses packages and classes. Related: Pascal units, C separate compilation, Java import statement; modular design aids reuse and testing.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct about modular programming approach?
 I. Ease of use
 II. Reusability
qs.sol: Modular programming is an approach in which a program is divided into smaller, independent modules. This makes the program easier to understand, use, test, and maintain. Since these modules can also be used again in the same or other programs, reusability is also an important advantage. Therefore, both statement I and statement II are correct.
qs.rel: Modular approach benefits: ease of use/understanding, reusability, testability, maintenance. Neighbouring facts: a module is also called function, subroutine or macro; modules communicate via parameters and interfaces.

qs.stem: In a modular programming approach problem is further divided into _____.
qs.sol: Modular programming is a design technique where complex problems are broken down into smaller, manageable parts. These distinct functional units are specifically called modules within the programming paradigm.
qs.rel: A problem is divided into modules in modular (top-down) design. Neighbouring facts: top-down starts with the main module and refines; bottom-up (OOP) builds small parts first; the steps end with revise and resequence.

qs.stem: In modular programming, the data items passed (or communicated) are called ______.
qs.sol: Data passed between modules through a call or interface are parameters. They carry values into the receiving module.
qs.rel: Values passed between modules are parameters (actual in the call, formal in the definition). Related: pass by value vs by reference vs by address; return values also communicate results.

qs.stem: What is responsibility of event queue in event driven programming?

opts.C: Make a sequence in which event is executed

qs.sol: The event queue stores and manages events waiting for processing. Its core responsibility is organizing these events into a specific order to ensure sequential execution based on arrival or priority.
qs.rel: Event queue keeps events in order for execution; event loop dispatches them. Related: queue is FIFO; handlers are callbacks; events are produced by sources (user, sensor, system).

qs.stem:
Which of the following is a type of subprogram?
 I. Functions
 II. Subroutines
qs.sol: In computer science, both functions and subroutines are standard classifications of subprograms used to modularize code effectively. Functions typically return values, while subroutines perform specific actions without necessarily returning a value, yet both fall under the broader category of subprograms in programming theory.
qs.rel: Subprograms are functions (return a value) and subroutines/procedures. Related: VB has Sub and Function; C functions returning void act as procedures; both support modularity.

qs.stem: One very useful way modules can interact is through ______.
qs.sol: A module interface exposes the operations or data through which modules communicate while hiding internal implementation.
qs.rel: Modules interact through an interface (parameters and return values). Related: coupling should be low and cohesion high; global data increases coupling; information hiding keeps internals private.

qs.stem: The ability to group some lines of code into a unit that can be included in program is called ______.
qs.sol: Modularisation groups related code into a reusable unit or module that a program can include.
qs.rel: Grouping code into a reusable unit is modularisation. Related: functions, procedures, macros, classes; supports reuse, testability, and abstraction.

qs.stem: Models having the concept of event-driven programming are called ______.
qs.sol: Event-driven programs react when events arrive, rather than following a fixed synchronous call sequence. The model is asynchronous.
qs.rel: Event-driven programs are asynchronous: they react to events, not fixed call order. Related: event loop, queue, handlers; GUI, web and IoT use this model; callbacks drive control flow.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about event-handler in an event-driven programming? 
(i) It is a call back routine. 
(ii) It operates asynchronously.
qs.sol: Event handlers are callback routines triggered by specific events, making statement (i) true. They operate asynchronously without blocking the main thread, confirming statement (ii). Thus, both statements accurately describe event-driven programming.
qs.rel: Event handlers are callback routines that run asynchronously when events occur. Related: registered with listener/subscription; 'listener' waits, 'handler' acts; must be short to avoid blocking.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a paradigm where entities (objects, services, and so on) communicate indirectly by sending messages to one another through an intermediary?
qs.sol: In event-driven programming, components publish or send events through an intermediary and other components react. This allows indirect communication.
qs.rel: Event-driven systems communicate indirectly via events through an intermediary. Related: publish-subscribe, message broker, queue; producers and consumers are decoupled.

qs.stem: In event-driven programming, server and client programs interact with each other through ______.
qs.sol: Message queues hold messages between producers and consumers. They let server and client programs interact asynchronously.
qs.rel: Message queues carry events between producers and consumers asynchronously. Related: FIFO order; brokers (RabbitMQ, Kafka); dead letter queues hold failed messages.

qs.stem:
Which of the following options best describes the truthfulness of given statements with reference to modular programming?

(i) Other names for module are function, macro, sub-routine.

(ii) Two main categories modules are program control, specific task.
qs.sol: Functions, macros and subroutines are names used for program modules. The stated division into program-control and specific-task modules is also accepted here; both statements are true.
qs.rel: Module is also known as function, macro, subroutine. Related: main categories are program-control modules and specific-task modules; each module hides implementation.

qs.stem: With reference to event driven programming, when an event fails to be processed even after several retries, it is then posted to _
qs.sol: After repeated processing failures, an event is moved to a dead letter queue for inspection or later handling.
qs.rel: Events failing after retries go to a dead letter queue. Related: allows later inspection and replay; retry with backoff; poison messages.

qs.stem: An event-driven program is a program in which the flow of control of the program depends upon the ______.
qs.sol: Event-driven programs rely on external stimuli like user inputs or system signals to dictate execution paths. Instead of linear sequences, the flow changes dynamically based on these occurring events.
qs.rel: Event-driven flow depends on occurrence of external events. Related: user actions, sensors, messages; event loop; contrast with sequential flow.

qs.stem: When the same event needs to be handled by multiple entities, which of the following methods is used in even-driven programming?
qs.sol: Event splitting distributes one incoming event to multiple handlers, allowing each entity to process it.
qs.rel: Event splitting delivers one event to multiple handlers. Related: publish-subscribe fan-out; event aggregation merges many into one; filtering and routing.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about event in an event-driven programming?

opts.A: It is piece of data sent by producers.
opts.B: It is piece of data that may be consumed by consumers.
opts.C: An event does not occur when a key is pressed.
opts.D: An event occurs when the left mouse button is clicked.

qs.sol: Events are signals generated by user actions or system changes. A key press generates a keyboard event, making the statement that it does not occur incorrect.
qs.rel: A key press is an event; events are data sent by producers and consumed by consumers. Related: event types (mouse, keyboard, timer); event queue; handlers.

qs.stem:
Rearrange steps involved in top-down design programming? 

I. Analyze the problem 

II. Revise and resequence 

III. Write the main module

IV. Connect the modules in proper order 

V. Write the remaining modules
qs.sol:
I. Analyze the problem (Understand the requirements and goals first.)

III. Write the main module (Define the overall structure and control logic.)

V. Write the remaining modules (Break the main task into smaller, specialized sub-tasks.)

IV. Connect the modules in proper order (Integrate the sub-tasks so they work together.)

II. Revise and resequence (Test, debug, and refine the logic.)
qs.rel: Top-down design: analyse the problem, write the main module, write remaining modules, connect them in order, revise and resequence. Related: stepwise refinement; stubs; testing each module.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about event-loop in an event-driven programming?

opts.A: It performs two functions in a continuous loop.
opts.B: Its event-detection function detects the happening of an event.
opts.C: Its event-handler function executes the corresponding function associated with that event.
opts.D: It is a looping statement that is used to generate the same events repeatedly.

qs.sol: The event loop continuously monitors and processes events from sources rather than generating identical events repeatedly. Options A, B, and C describe standard behaviors accurately. Option D falsely claims the loop generates the same events repeatedly, making it the incorrect statement and the right choice.
qs.rel: The event loop detects and dispatches events; it does not generate identical ones. Related: two functions in a loop; blocking wait; handlers called per event.

qs.stem: Match the following with respect to Event Driven Programming.
qs.sol:
Modified from the official paper: the official keyed matching reverses event listener and event handler; the logically correct pairing is retained.

Concept

Event-driven programming separates three distinct roles. An event is the occurrence itself — something the user or the system does, such as a mouse click or a key press. An event listener is the registered piece of code that watches for occurrences of that kind and is notified when one happens. An event handler is the code that carries out the response once that notification arrives. Watching and responding are two different jobs held by two different pieces of code.

Application

i. …
qs.note: Table/figure from the original paper was not captured. Use the explanation to see the correct matching.
qs.rel: Event listener waits for events, event handler responds, event emitter produces them. Related: callbacks, event loop; the official key swaps listener/handler.

qs.stem: In Java, which event class is fired when a button is pressed?
qs.sol: An AWT or Swing button normally emits an ActionEvent when activated. A registered ActionListener receives that event and runs the button action.

qs.stem: Variables which can be accessed by all modules of the program is called —
qs.sol:
Correct answer: Queue

The statement describes the FIFO operation pattern of a queue: insertion happens at the rear and deletion happens from the front.

Queue: this is the abstract data structure defined by enqueue at the rear and dequeue from the front.

Linked list: this is an implementation structure. A linked list can be used to implement a queue, but a linked list by itself does not enforce this rear/front FIFO rule.

Stack: this follows LIFO behavior, where insertion and deletion happen at the same end.

So only queue directly matches the behavior asked in the question.

qs.stem: Variables which can be accessed by all modules of the program is called —
qs.sol: Variables that can be accessed by all modules of a program are known as global variables. These variables are declared outside any function or block and are accessible throughout the entire program.Auto variables are created within a function and are destroyed when the function ends. They are not accessible outside the function, so they cannot be accessed by all modules.Static variables retain their value between function calls but are typically limited to the file or function scope unless explicitly declared as global. They are not accessible across all modules by default.Local variables are confined to the function or block in which they are declared. …

qs.stem: Among the following, which statement is correct about the modularity?

opts.A: Modularity means hiding the parts of the program
opts.B: Modularity refers to dividing a program into subsequent small modules or independent parts
opts.C: It refers to overloading the program’s part
opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: Modularity in programming refers to the practice of dividing a program into smaller, independent modules or components. Each module performs a specific function and can be developed, tested, and maintained separately. This approach enhances code readability, reusability, and maintainability. It allows developers to focus on individual parts without affecting the entire system. Modularity is a key principle in software design, enabling better organization and scalability of programs.

The correct design principle is Low Coupling.

In software engineering, coupling refers to the degree of interdependence between software modules. Low coupling means that modules are independent and changes in one module do not significantly affect others. This ensures minimal dependency, making the system easier to maintain and modify.

High cohesion (Option A) refers to how closely related the responsibilities within a single module are, which is a separate concept. Encapsulation (Option D) focuses on hiding internal details, and tight binding is not a standard principle for reducing dependencies. …

During program execution, certain events can interrupt the normal flow of instructions. These events are handled using a specific mechanism in programming that allows the program to respond to unexpected conditions without crashing.

The mechanism involves detecting an abnormal condition, pausing the current execution, and transferring control to a special block of code designed to handle the issue. This allows the program to recover gracefully or terminate safely.

This concept is fundamental in error handling and ensures robustness in software. It is used in many programming languages to manage runtime errors such as division by zero, file not found, or invalid input. …

qs.stem: Which programming paradigm focuses on breaking down a program into smaller procedures or functions?
qs.sol: Evaluate the inner parentheses first: −3−3=−6. Then 3−(−6)−3 = 3+6−3 = 6.

qs.stem: Which programming paradigm focuses on breaking down a program into smaller procedures or functions?
qs.sol: Procedural Programming organizes a program into procedures or functions and executes steps in sequence. Object-Oriented Programming organizes code around objects and classes. Functional Programming emphasizes function evaluation and composition, while Imperative Programming describes state-changing commands.

qs.stem: Which language is better for writing structured code?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
PASCAL is designed with strong support for structured programming concepts like procedures, functions, and clear control structures. It enforces disciplined coding practices, making it suitable for writing structured code.

FORTRAN is primarily optimized for numerical and scientific computing. It lacks modern structured programming constructs, making it less suitable for general structured code development.

BASIC is a simple language with limited support for structured programming. It often relies on GOTO statements, which can lead to unstructured code.

Since only PASCAL supports structured programming among the given options, 'More than one of the above' is incorrect. …

Coupling measures the degree of interdependence between modules.

Cohesion measures how closely related the functions within a module are.

Good software design aims for:
 Low coupling (modules are independent)

High cohesion (each module does one well-defined task)

topics.deep:
- **Modular programming:** decompose a large problem into small **modules** (functions, procedures, subroutines, macros; classes/packages at a higher level). Advantages: easier to design, understand, **test** and debug each unit, **reusability**, team division of labour, localised maintenance. Disadvantage: interface overhead.
- **Module qualities:** *cohesion* (high is good - one module, one job) and *coupling* (low is good - few dependencies). Modules interact only through an **interface** (parameters / return values); hiding internals is information hiding.
- **Module categories:** program-control modules (decide flow) and specific-task modules; also library modules. Names for module: function, subroutine, procedure, macro, method.
- **Support:** C (functions, header files, separate compilation), C++ (headers, namespaces, classes), Java (packages, classes), Pascal (units).
- **Parameters:** *actual* (in the call) vs *formal* (in the definition). Pass by value, by reference, by address (pointer).
- **Subprograms:** *function* returns a value; *subroutine/procedure* performs actions (VB `Sub` vs `Function`).
- **Structured/top-down design steps:** 1. analyse the problem; 2. write the main module; 3. write the remaining (subordinate) modules; 4. connect the modules in proper order; 5. revise and resequence. Bottom-up design builds low-level modules first (OOP is bottom-up).
- **Event-driven programming (EDP):** control flow is decided by **events**: user actions (click, key press), sensor input, messages. Typical GUI/web/IoT model. Sequence is not predetermined; the program *waits*, then reacts - hence **asynchronous**.
- **EDP components:**

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| Event producer / emitter | creates the event (data about what happened) |
| Event queue | holds events and orders them for processing (FIFO) |
| Event loop | repeatedly (1) detects events and (2) dispatches them |
| Event handler / listener | callback routine run when its event occurs; registered with the source |
| Event consumer | receives and acts on the event |
| Message broker / message queue | intermediary for indirect communication |

- **Reliability patterns:** retry on failure; if an event still fails after several retries it is moved to a **dead letter queue** for later inspection. **Event splitting** sends a single event to several handlers; publish/subscribe delivers to all subscribers; event merging/aggregation combines events.
- **Callback:** function passed to be called later; event handlers are callbacks (hence "callback routine"). JavaScript `button.addEventListener("click", fn)` and VB `Private Sub cmdOK_Click(...)` are examples.
- **Procedural vs event-driven:** procedural = fixed order of statements controlled by the programmer; event-driven = order depends on external events.
- **Programming paradigms:** imperative/procedural, object-oriented (organises design around objects and data), declarative (SQL, Prolog), functional (LISP, Haskell), scripting, rule-based, event-driven.
- **Common traps:** event queue *orders* events, it does not create, delete or change them; event loop *consumes* events, it does not generate them; handler is not synchronous in the sense of blocking the main thread.
- **Likely question angles:**
  - Identify the cohesion/coupling property that makes a good module.
  - Order the steps of top-down design given a shuffled list.
  - Classify C/Java/VB features as modular constructs (namespace, package, header, unit).
  - Name the structure that stores pending events / what the dead letter queue holds.
  - True/false: event handler blocks the main thread; event loop generates events.
  - Which paradigm is used for GUI applications; which for SQL.
  - Difference between function and subroutine; actual vs formal parameter.
  - Output of a small callback snippet that registers handlers and fires events in order.
  - Name three benefits of modular design.

topics.title: 3. C/C++ Tokens, Operators, Control Flow & Output Prediction
topics.theory:
- **Identifiers:** letters, digits, underscore; cannot start with a digit; cannot be a **keyword** (`void`, `volatile`, `static` are keywords; `integer`, `automatic`, `constant` are not).
- **Statement terminator** in C/C++ is the semicolon `;`. `bool` holds only **two** values (true/false). Wide-character literal prefix = **`L`** (`L'a'`).
- **Arithmetic:** `%` takes the **sign of the dividend** (`7 % -3 = 1`, `-7 % 3 = -1`); integer division truncates (`8/9 = 0`). **Relational/logical** results are `1` or `0`; `&&` short-circuits.
- **Increment:** `x++` uses value then increments; `++x` increments then uses. Modifying a variable twice without a sequence point is **undefined behaviour**.
- **Bitwise:** `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` (`5 & 7 = 5`); `x ^ x = 0`. **Comma operator** evaluates left to right, value = last operand.
- **Assignment** `=` is **right-to-left** associative; ternary `?:` (conditional operator) cannot be overloaded.
- **Literals:** `62` decimal, `062` octal (=50), `0x62` hex (=98). `printf` returns the **number of characters printed**.
- **switch:** without `break` execution **falls through** to following cases; code after `break` in the same block is unreachable. `for(i=0;i<5;i++)` runs 5 times.
- **I/O:** `cout` is an object of **`ostream`**; `<<` = insertion, `>>` = extraction; `namespace` defines a scope for identifiers; `main()` is user-defined, but its name is fixed.
- **Loops in C:** `for`, `while`, `do-while` only (no foreach); `void` = no return value / empty parameter list.

qs.sol: Standard C provides for, while and do-while statements. It has no foreach statement, so foreach loop is the requested construct.
qs.rel: C has only for, while, do-while; C++11 adds range-based for, Java has enhanced for-each. do-while runs the body at least once. Also asked: which loop is entry-controlled (for, while) versus exit-controlled (do-while).

qs.sol: C arithmetic operators include remainder, addition, and subtraction. The token \(&&\) performs logical conjunction, so it belongs to logical operators.
qs.rel: Operator categories in C: arithmetic (+ - * / %), relational, logical (&& || !), bitwise, assignment, conditional. Related: % needs integers, && and || short-circuit, and bitwise & differs from logical &&.

qs.stem: Which of the following characters is a terminal that terminates a statement in C++?
qs.sol: In C++, every executable statement must end with a semicolon (;). This symbol signals the compiler that the command is complete before proceeding to the next line of code.
qs.rel: Every C/C++ statement ends with a semicolon, which terminates it. Related: a missing semicolon is a syntax error; a stray semicolon after for/if creates an empty body; Java method headers also take no semicolon.

qs.stem: In C++, bool data type is used to hold how many values?
qs.sol:
In C++, the bool data type is used to store only two possible values:

true

false

Since it can hold only these two values, the correct answer is 2.
qs.rel: C++ bool stores true or false (two values), typically 1 byte, printed as 1/0 unless boolalpha is used. Related: any non-zero value converts to true; sizeof(bool) is implementation-defined, usually 1.

qs.sol: C reserves void as a keyword denoting absence of a value. A keyword cannot be used as an identifier, whereas the other strings meet identifier rules.
qs.rel: Keywords such as void cannot be used as identifiers. Related: C has 32 keywords (int, float, volatile, static ...); valid identifiers can start with underscore; case-sensitive so Int is not int.

qs.stem:
Which statement(s) is/are true about formation of identifier in C?
 I. It consist of alphabets, digits and underscore.
 II. An identifier can start with an underscore.
qs.sol: C identifiers allow alphabets, digits, and underscores only. They may start with an underscore but not a digit. Both statements correctly reflect these standard C syntax rules.
qs.rel: C identifier: letters, digits, underscore; may start with underscore not digit. Related: case-sensitive; reserved words excluded; only first 31 chars significant in older standards.

qs.sol: After a matching case runs, execution proceeds into the next case labels when no break is present. It continues until another break or the closing brace of the switch is reached.
qs.rel: Without break, switch falls through to subsequent cases until a break or the end. Related: default can appear anywhere; nested switch break exits only the inner switch; case labels must be constants.

qs.stem: cout is a predefined object of the ______ class.
qs.sol:
Concept: In C++ every console read or write travels through a stream class declared by the <iostream> family of headers. The library defines two narrow-character stream types with opposite directions: istream (the typedef for basic_istream<char>) models a stream that extracts characters from a source, and ostream (the typedef for basic_ostream<char>) models a stream that inserts characters into a destination. A predefined stream object is an instance of one of these classes, and the class it instantiates fixes both the direction of data flow and the operators the object supports.

Application: Including <iostream> automatically declares the standard stream objects. …
qs.rel: cout is an object of ostream (cin of istream), declared in <iostream>. Related: cerr and clog are also ostream objects; << is insertion, >> is extraction; endl flushes.

qs.sol: The loop starts at zero and runs while i<5. It executes for i=0,1,2,3,4, then the increment makes i=5 and the condition fails.
qs.rel: For loop i=0; i<5; i++ iterates five times (0..4) and ends with i=5. Related: semicolon after for gives empty body; infinite loop forms; loop variable scope in for-init.

qs.sol: An automatic local variable that has not been initialized holds an indeterminate value. Reading it does not inherently produce a compile-time diagnostic or a guaranteed runtime exception, and C does not automatically assign zero to such a local object. The observed value is therefore unspecified and commonly described as garbage.
qs.rel: An uninitialised automatic (local) variable holds garbage. Related: globals and statics default to zero; reading garbage is undefined behaviour; always initialise.

qs.stem: Which statement is NOT correct regarding ternary operator in C++?

opts.B: It is also known as conditional operator
opts.C: Operator overloading is possible in it
opts.D: It is similar to if else

qs.sol:
The ternary operator in C++ is represented by ?: and is also called the conditional operator. It behaves similarly to an if-else statement by evaluating a condition and selecting one of two expressions.

In C++, the ternary operator cannot be overloaded. Therefore, the statement “Operator overloading is possible in it” is NOT correct.
qs.rel: Ternary ?: is the conditional operator, similar to if-else, and cannot be overloaded. Related: other non-overloadable ones are ::, ., .*, sizeof; it is right-associative.

qs.sol:
The declaration has three declarators. The initializer is attached only to c, so 
𝑐
=
10
c=10, while a and b are declared without initializers and have indeterminate automatic values.

The declaration is valid C syntax because an initializer may appear on one declarator in a comma-separated declaration.
qs.rel: int a, b, c = 10; initialises only c; a and b are indeterminate. Related: each declarator has its own initialiser; in a pointer declaration * binds to each name.

qs.sol: In Java, a break statement immediately exits the switch block. Any code following a break within the same case block is unreachable because execution terminates before reaching it.
qs.rel: Statements after break in the same case block are unreachable. Related: without break execution falls through; compiler warns of unreachable code in Java (an error).

qs.stem: n C++, namespace defines a _____ for the identifiers that are used in a program.
qs.rel: A namespace defines a scope for identifiers, avoiding name clashes. Related: using namespace std; scope operator std::cout; anonymous namespaces; nested namespaces.

qs.stem: In C++, operator  >>  is used along with object  cin  for reading input is known as _____.
qs.sol:
In C++, the >> operator used with the cin object is called the extraction operator because it extracts input from the keyboard/input stream and stores it into variables.

Example:

While (p! = 0)
{
If (p>q)
p=p-q;

q=q-p;

qs.sol:
At p = q > 0, the else branch sets q to zero while p stays positive.

In every later iteration p > q and p = p − 0, so p does not change.

The test p != 0 therefore remains true forever.

Concept

The subtraction form of the Euclidean algorithm preserves the greatest common divisor: if a > b, then gcd(a, b) = gcd(a - b, b), and similarly when b > a.

For positive integers, repeatedly reducing the larger value must eventually make the two values equal. Their common value is the GCD of the original inputs.

Application

Take p = 18 and q = 12. Since p > q, the first update gives (p, q) = (6, 12).

Now q > p, so q becomes 12 - 6 = 6, giving (p, q) = (6, 6).

The condition p != q is now false, so the loop stops and printf outputs 6.

Cross-check

The common divisors of 18 and 12 are 1, 2, 3, and 6; the greatest is 6, which matches the traced output. …

topics.deep:
- **Character set and tokens:** keywords, identifiers, constants (literals), strings, operators, punctuators. **Identifier rules (C/C++/Java):** start with letter or `_` (Java also `$`), then letters/digits/`_`; no spaces, no keywords; case-sensitive. C keywords (32): `auto break case char const continue default do double else enum extern float for goto if int long register return short signed sizeof static struct switch typedef union unsigned void volatile while`. `integer`, `automatic`, `constant` are **not** keywords.
- **Fundamental types (typical 64-bit):**

| Type | Size (bytes) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| char | 1 | `'A'` = 65 |
| short | 2 | |
| int | 4 | |
| long | 4 (Windows) / 8 (Linux) | |
| float | 4 | ~7 digits |
| double | 8 | ~15 digits |
| bool (C++) | 1 | only true/false |
| wchar_t | 2/4 | literal `L'a'` |

- **Operator precedence (high to low):** `() [] -> .` > postfix `++ --` > unary `! ~ + - ++ -- * & sizeof` > `* / %` > `+ -` > `<< >>` > `< <= > >=` > `== !=` > `&` > `^` > `|` > `&&` > `||` > `?:` > `= += -= ...` > `,`. Assignment and ?: are **right-to-left**; the rest mostly left-to-right.
- **Arithmetic:** `5/2 = 2`, `5/2.0 = 2.5`, `-7/2 = -3`; `%` sign follows dividend: `7 % -3 = 1`, `-7 % 3 = -1`. `%` needs integers.
- **Relational/logical:** results are `1` or `0`. `10 > 5 > 2` -> `(1) > 2` -> `0`. `!5` = 0. `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: `0 && x++` never evaluates `x++`.
- **Increment:** `x = 5; y = x++;` -> y=5, x=6. `y = ++x;` -> x=6, y=6. `z = x++ + 17` with x=33 -> z=50, x=34. Modifying a variable twice in one expression (`i = i++ + ++i`) is **undefined**.
- **Bitwise:** `5 & 7 = 5`, `5 | 2 = 7`, `5 ^ 5 = 0`, `~5 = -6`, `1 << 3 = 8`. `!(x ^ y)` is true when x == y.
- **Comma operator:** `k = (v = 20, v + 2);` -> k = 22. **Compound assignment:** `x += 3` same as `x = x + 3`.
- **Literals:** `62` dec, `062` octal = 50, `0x62` hex = 98; `printf("%d%d%d",62,062,0x62)` prints `625098`. `'A'` char constant is `int` in C.
- **printf return value:** number of characters printed: `printf("%d", printf("Tata Consultancy"))` prints `Tata Consultancy16`. `%d`, `%f`, `%c`, `%s`, `%x`, `%o`, `%p`.
- **Control flow:** `if/else`, `?:`, `switch` (integer/char cases, `default`, `break`), loops `for / while / do-while` (do-while runs at least once). No `foreach` in C; C++11 has range-for.
- **Switch fall-through:** `switch(2){case 1:printf("a"); case 2:printf("b"); case 3:printf("c"); break; default:printf("d");}` prints `bc`. Code after `break` in a case is unreachable. Nested switch: inner `break` leaves only the inner switch.
- **Loop traps:** `for(i=0;i<3;i++);` (semicolon) -> empty body, then `i` is 3. `for(i=1;i<=10;i++)` with `i++` inside body too -> skips values. `while(i++ < 3)` increments even when test fails.
- **C++ I/O:** `cin >> x` (extraction), `cout << x` (insertion), `cerr`, `clog`; `cout` is an object of class `ostream`, `cin` of `istream`; both in `<iostream>`, namespace `std`. `endl` = newline + flush. `namespace` gives a scope to identifiers and avoids name clashes; `using namespace std;`.
- **Conditional expression:** `grade = marks >= 90 ? 'A' : marks >= 70 ? 'B' : 'C';` with 75 gives `B`. `?:` is the only ternary, cannot be overloaded.
- **Uninitialised variables:** `int a, b, c = 10;` only `c` is initialised.
- **Likely question angles:**
  - Output of `printf("%d", 7 % -3)`, `printf("%d", 10 > 5 > 2)`, `printf("%d", 5 & 3)`.
  - Output of a snippet with `x++ + ++x`-free pre/post increments (e.g. `x=5; y=x++*2; printf("%d %d",x,y)` -> `6 10`).
  - Result of a switch with missing `break` or nested switches.
  - Valid vs invalid identifier (`2abc`, `_x`, `my-var`, `for`).
  - Size of data types, or value of `sizeof(char)`, `sizeof(int)`.
  - Octal/hex literal output, `printf("%c", 65)`, `printf("%d", 'a')`.
  - Associativity/precedence puzzle: `a = b = 5`, `2 + 3 * 4 % 5`.
  - Do-while vs while: how many times does the body run when the condition is initially false?
  - Which operators cannot be overloaded; which is the extraction/insertion operator.

topics.title: 4. Functions, Pointers, Arrays, Strings & File Handling
topics.theory:
- **Prototype** declares return type, function name and number/types of parameters; **default arguments** are filled right-to-left (`sum(20,30)` with `b=10,c=20` = 20+30+20).
- **C passes arguments by value**: changing a pointer parameter inside a function does not change the caller's pointer; passing an array passes its address, so changes persist.
- **Pointer basics:** `int *p = &x;` `*p` = indirection (dereference); `p = q` makes both point to the same object; `PTR = &C` is valid, `PTR = C` is not. Type must match (`double *fp = &int_var` is invalid).
- **Pointer arithmetic** moves in units of the pointed type; `p++` then `p--` returns to start; arithmetic on `void *` is not allowed; `*(arr+i)` = `arr[i]` = `i[arr]`.
- **Declarators:** `int *a[5]` = array of 5 int pointers; `int (*a)[5]` = pointer to array of 5 ints; `int (*f)(char*)` = pointer to function taking `char*` returning int; `int (*p[5])()` = array of 5 function pointers.
- **Arrays:** 0-indexed; `sizeof(arr)` = elements x element size; `int a[2][2]={1,2,3,4}` fills row by row; array name converts to pointer to first element.
- **NULL pointer** compares unequal to any valid object; uninitialised local variables hold indeterminate (garbage) values.
- **Files (C):** `FILE *fp = fopen(name,"r")` returns NULL on failure; `fclose(fp)`. **C++ streams:** `ifstream` (input), `ofstream` (output), `fstream` (both); modes `ios::in`, `ios::out`, `ios::app` (append), `ios::ate`.
- **Storage:** `struct` members laid out sequentially, `union` members share memory (size = largest member).
- ISO C does not allow nested functions (GCC extension only); `puts` writes a string, `gets/cgets` reads a string.

qs.sol: A C stream opened with fopen is represented by FILE*. fclose(fp) flushes buffered output as needed and closes that stream.
qs.rel: C file handling uses FILE * from fopen, closed by fclose which flushes buffers. Related: fopen returns NULL on failure; modes r, w, a, r+; fgets/fputs/fprintf/fscanf are the I/O calls.

qs.sol:
Concept: In a C declaration, each declarator has its own pointer marker. The type of an assignment expression is checked from the types of its left and right operands.

The address-of operator produces a pointer to its operand type; dereferencing an int pointer produces an int lvalue. A pointer value is distinct from the int value at the pointed-to address.

Application:

Read int C, *PTR; declarator by declarator: C has type int, while PTR has type int * (pointer to int).

Apply & to C: because C has type int, &C has type int * and denotes C’s address.

Compare the assignment operands: PTR has type int * and &C has type int *, so PTR = &C; assigns that address to the pointer. …
qs.rel: PTR = &C assigns the address of C to a pointer. Related: *PTR = C stores a value; PTR = C is a type error; C = &PTR is invalid.

qs.stem: Considering A as a one-dimensional array, which of the following C++ statements will print the third element of A?
qs.sol:
Concept

In C and C++, array indexing is zero-based: the element at position k (counting from 1) lives at index k - 1. The subscript operator is also commutative, because a[i] is defined as *(a + i); since addition commutes, a[i] equals i[a] for any array a and integer i.

Applying it here

The third element is at index 3 - 1 = 2, i.e. A[2].

By commutativity of the subscript, A[2] is the same as 2[A], both expanding to *(A + 2).

To send a value to standard output you use the insertion operator <<, so cout << 2[A]; prints that element. …
qs.rel: Arrays are zero-based, so the third element is A[2], also written 2[A] since A[i] is *(A+i). Related: cout << A[3] gives the fourth; >> with cout is invalid.

qs.sol: ISO standard C defines functions only at file scope. Some compilers, notably GNU C, allow nested function definitions as an extension.
qs.rel: ISO C has no nested functions; GCC permits them as an extension. Related: functions are defined at file scope; function pointers; static functions are file-local.

qs.stem: The operator in C++, which is used to access a value referred by a pointer is known as ______.
qs.rel: * is the indirection (dereference) operator. Related: & is address-of; -> accesses members through a pointer; pointer to pointer needs **.

qs.sol:
Concept: A C null pointer is a pointer value guaranteed to compare unequal to a pointer to any object or function.

A pointer should hold a valid target address or an explicit null value before code tries to use it; a null check can guard dereference. Setting one pointer to NULL does not fix other aliases.

Consider int *p = NULL;. The initializer gives p the null pointer value, so p refers to no object.

A condition such as p != NULL is false. The guarded dereference is therefore skipped until p receives a valid object address.

If an allocated object is freed, assigning p = NULL replaces p’s stale address; any separate aliases must be handled independently. …
qs.rel: A null pointer is guaranteed unequal to any valid object address. Related: NULL is 0 in C++ (nullptr in C++11); dereferencing it is undefined; malloc returns NULL on failure.
