topics.deep:
- **Functions:** declaration (prototype) `int sum(int a, int b);` tells the compiler return type, name, and number/types of parameters before the definition. Definition has a body. C does **not** allow nested function definitions in ISO C (GCC allows as extension). In C++ default arguments are given **right to left**: `int sum(int a, int b=10, int c=20)`; `sum(20,30)` = 20+30+20 = 70; `sum(1)` = 31.
- **Parameter passing:** C is always **pass by value**. To change the caller's variable, pass its address: `void swap(int *a,int *b){int t=*a;*a=*b;*b=t;}`. C++ adds **references** (`int &a`). An array parameter decays to a pointer, so the callee changes the caller's array. Assigning to a pointer parameter (`p = &q`) changes only the local copy.
- **Pointers:** `int x = 5, *p = &x;` `*p` -> 5; `&x` address; `p++` moves `sizeof(int)` bytes. `int **q = &p;` -> `**q` = 5. Swap via pointers without temp: `*p1 = *p1 + *p2; *p2 = *p1 - *p2; *p1 = *p1 - *p2;` (a=10,b=20 -> a=20,b=10). Pointer to pointer example: `a=3; p=&a; q=&p; b = 2*(**q + *p)` = 12.
- **Declaration reading (inside-out):**

| Declaration | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `int *p` | p is pointer to int |
| `int *a[5]` | array of 5 pointers to int |
| `int (*a)[5]` | pointer to array of 5 int |
| `int (*f)(char*)` | pointer to function(char*) returning int |
| `int (*p[5])()` | array of 5 pointers to function returning int |
| `int *f(int)` | function returning pointer to int |
| `const int *p` | pointer to const int |
| `int *const p` | const pointer to int |

- **Pointer rules:** `int c, *ptr; ptr = &c;` valid; `ptr = c;` and `*ptr = &c;` invalid. `int *p, q;` declares q as plain `int`. `int *ptr=0, p;` is legal. `double *fp = &intvar;` invalid in C++ (type mismatch). `void *` is generic: no arithmetic, no dereference without cast. NULL pointer is never equal to a valid object address. Dereferencing NULL/uninitialised pointer is undefined.
- **Arrays:** `int arr[5]` -> indices 0..4; `sizeof(arr)` = 20 (4-byte int); `arr` converts to `&arr[0]`; `arr[i]` = `*(arr+i)` = `i[arr]`, so `cout << 2[A]` prints the third element. `int a[2][2]={1,2,3,4}` -> `a[0]={1,2}, a[1]={3,4}`. Array of C strings: `char *str[]={"one","two","three"}; str[2][4]` = `'e'`. Pointer walk: `ptr=num; ptr++; ptr-=1; *ptr` -> `num[0]`. `int (*p)[5]=&arr; *(*p+3)` -> `arr[3]`.
- **Strings (C):** char array ending in `'�'`; `strlen` excludes it; `gets`/`cgets` read a string (unsafe), `puts` writes one, `getchar` reads one char. `char a[10]; for(i=0;i<5;i++) *(a+i)=65+i; a[i]='\0'; cout<<a;` prints `ABCDE`.
- **struct/union sizes:** `struct` = sum of members (+padding); `union` = largest member. Example: `struct{short a[5]; union{float f; long l;} u;}` with short=2, float=4, long=8 -> 10 + 8 = 18 bytes (ignoring padding), because the union takes its largest member.
- **C file I/O:** `FILE *fp = fopen("test.txt","r"); if(fp==NULL) ... else ...; fclose(fp);` modes `r, w, a, r+, w+, a+`; `fopen` returns NULL on failure; `fclose` flushes the buffer. `fgets, fputs, fprintf, fscanf, fread, fwrite, fseek, ftell, feof`.
- **C++ streams (`<fstream>`):** `ifstream` input only, `ofstream` output only, `fstream` both, `fstreambase` is the common base. Mode flags: `ios::in` (read), `ios::out` (write, truncates), `ios::app` (append at end, keeps contents), `ios::ate` (go to end on open), `ios::trunc`, `ios::binary`. Combine with `|`.
- **Preprocessor:** `#include` replaces the directive with the file contents; `#define` macro substitution; it does not replace escape sequences or check types.
- **Pointers and strings output example:** `int a=10,b=20,*p1=&a,*p2=&b;` after swap-without-temp prints `After : **p1=20 **p2=10` style output (values swapped).
- **Common traps:** `sizeof` on an array parameter gives pointer size; `i[arr]` is legal; `p = q` copies the address, not the value; forgetting `&` in `scanf`; returning a pointer to a local variable; NULL vs uninitialised pointer.
- **Likely question angles:**
  - Output of snippets with pointer arithmetic: `int a[]={10,20,30}; int *p=a; printf("%d", *(p+2));` -> 30.
  - Interpret a declaration (`int *(*f)(int)`, `char **argv`).
  - Valid/invalid pointer assignment statements.
  - Size of struct vs union; `sizeof` of arrays and pointers.
  - What happens if a function modifies its parameter (value vs address).
  - Which `ios` flag opens for reading / appending; difference ifstream/ofstream/fstream.
  - What `fopen` returns when the file does not exist.
  - Default arguments: which call is legal given `f(int a, int b=2, int c=3)`.
  - Output of a 2-D array initialisation printed row by row.

topics.title: 5. OOP Concepts (General)
topics.theory:
- **Four pillars:** **Encapsulation** (bind data + methods, hide data), **Abstraction** (show essentials, hide details), **Inheritance** (reuse/extend a class), **Polymorphism** (one interface, many forms). "Abduction" is not an OOP term.
- **Class** = blueprint/user-defined type with data members and member functions; **object** = **instance** of a class.
- **Data hiding** = private members inaccessible outside the class (achieved via encapsulation/access specifiers); abstraction = representing essential features without background details.
- **Inheritance** gives **reusability**: base/super/parent class -> derived/sub/child class. Types: single, multiple, multilevel, **hierarchical** (one base, many derived), hybrid.
- **Polymorphism:** compile-time (function/operator overloading) and run-time (virtual functions/overriding); lets objects with different internals share the same external interface.
- Objects communicate by **message passing** (calling methods); objects need not know each other's internals.
- OOP is **bottom-up**; data is central, not procedures; data does not move freely (it is protected).
- First OOP step: **data modelling** (identify objects and relationships).
- **OOP languages:** Simula (first), Smalltalk, C++, Java, Ruby, Emerald; LISP (functional), SQL (declarative) and C (procedural) are not primarily OOP.
- Operator overloading is **not** a feature of inheritance.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT an object oriented feature?
qs.sol:
OOP features include:

Inheritance: one class can derive from another class.

Abstraction: implementation details are hidden behind a simpler interface.

Polymorphism: the same operation can behave differently for different object types.

Encapsulation: data and methods are bundled together.

The word Abduction is related to reasoning/inference, not to OOP features.

Therefore, Abduction is the correct answer.
qs.rel: The four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism. Neighbouring asks: abstraction vs encapsulation, compile-time vs run-time polymorphism, which pillar gives reuse (inheritance).

qs.stem: What may be achieved by the inheritance feature of object-oriented programming?
qs.sol: Inheritance allows a class to derive properties and methods from another class. This mechanism primarily promotes code reusability by reducing redundancy in software development.
qs.rel: Inheritance gives code reusability through base/derived relationships. Related: a derived class can add or override members; polymorphism gives flexibility; encapsulation gives data security.

qs.stem: In C++, the class that inherits from another class is referred to as ______.
qs.sol:
In inheritance, the existing class supplies members to a new class.

The inheriting new class is the derived class.
qs.rel: The inheriting class is the derived (sub/child) class; the original is base (super/parent). Related: C++ syntax class D : public B; Java uses extends; constructors run base-first.

qs.stem: What is the relation between object and class in an object-oriented programming?
qs.rel: An object is an instance of a class (class = blueprint). Related: many objects per class; memory is allocated per object, not per class definition; creating an object is called instantiation.

qs.stem: Which of the following features of object-oriented programming is used to secure the data?
qs.sol: Encapsulation is the fundamental object-oriented programming concept designed to bundle data and methods while restricting direct access to internal components. This mechanism secures data by preventing unauthorized modification through access modifiers like private or protected.
qs.rel: Encapsulation (with access control) protects data by bundling it with methods and hiding it. Related: data hiding via private members; abstraction hides implementation complexity instead.

qs.stem:
There are three main concepts that any language needs to support to be an object-oriented language.
 Which of the following is one of them?
 I. Encapsulation
 II. Inheritance
 III. Polymorphism
qs.sol:
The three main concepts required for a language to support Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) are:

Encapsulation – Binding data and methods together into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access to data.

Inheritance – Allowing one class to acquire properties and methods of another class for code reusability.

Polymorphism – Allowing the same function or method to behave differently in different situations.

Since all three are core principles of OOP, the correct answer is I, II and III.
qs.rel: Core OOP concepts: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism (with abstraction often added). Related: a language lacking one of them is only 'object-based' (e.g. early Visual Basic).

qs.stem: Which of the following is known as a derived class with only one base class?
qs.sol:
Single inheritance gives one derived class exactly one direct base class.

The other terms describe several bases, levels, or derived branches.
qs.rel: Single inheritance means one base for one derived class. Related: multilevel is a chain A->B->C; multiple means several bases (diamond problem); hierarchical is one base with many derived; hybrid mixes them.

qs.stem: A/An ______ is a user-defined datatype which has data members and member functions.
qs.sol: In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), a class serves as a blueprint or a template for creating objects. It is considered a user-defined datatype because it allows a developer to group different types of data and operations together under one name.
qs.rel: A class is a user-defined data type bundling data members and member functions. Related: struct in C++ is the same with default public; object is an instance; method is a function inside a class.

qs.stem: Which of the following is the act of representing essential features without including the background details or explanations?
qs.sol:
Concept

Abstraction models an entity through the properties and operations relevant to a user or task.

An interface describes what can be done, while implementation details describe how it is done; separating these levels reduces the detail a user must manage.

Application

Consider a stack interface with push and pop operations: the user needs their behavior, not its internal storage layout.

The stack can store elements in an array or linked nodes while exposing the same operations. Its essential behavior stays visible and its implementation remains behind the interface.

The stem describes this separation between essential features and background details, which is data abstraction. …
qs.rel: Abstraction shows essential features, omitting background detail. Related: realised via abstract classes and interfaces; encapsulation is the packaging; data hiding is restricting access.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a computer programming model that organises software design around data, or objects, rather than functions and logics?
qs.sol:
Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects that combine data and behaviour.

Thus the printed description identifies Object-oriented.
qs.rel: OOP organises software around objects holding data and behaviour. Related: procedural organises around functions; declarative (SQL) states what, not how; scripting and rule-based are other styles.

qs.stem: Which of the following languages is NOT an Object-Oriented Programming language?
qs.sol:
The preview keys Ada; the item uses a narrow classification even though later Ada revisions support object-oriented features.

Thus the printed description identifies Ada.
qs.rel: Ada is usually classed as procedural/concurrent (OOP features only from Ada 95). Related: Ruby, Java, Emerald, Smalltalk, Simula are OOP; Pascal and C are procedural.

qs.stem: Which of the following is true with respect to object-oriented programming?

opts.B: It treats procedures as a critical element in program development
opts.C: Data moves freely around the program
opts.D: It does not model the real world problems

qs.sol:
Object-oriented programming builds systems from objects and classes, a bottom-up approach.

It emphasizes encapsulated data and behavior rather than free-flowing data or procedure-first decomposition.
qs.rel: OOP follows a bottom-up approach, with data hidden and protected. Related: procedural is top-down; emphasis on data rather than procedures; data does not move freely.

qs.stem: How do objects interact with each other in object-oriented programming?
qs.sol:
In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), objects interact with each other through message passing. One object sends a message to another object by calling its methods or requesting services.

This communication mechanism allows objects to work together while maintaining encapsulation and modularity.
qs.rel: Objects interact by message passing, i.e. invoking methods. Related: needs only the public interface; dynamic binding decides which method runs; encapsulation hides internals.

qs.stem: The first step in Object-Oriented Programming is to collect all the objects a programmer wants to manipulate and identify how they relate to each other. This is referred to as _____.
qs.sol:
Data modelling identifies objects and relationships as a representation of the problem domain.

Thus the printed description identifies data modelling.
qs.rel: First step of OOP design is data modelling: find objects and their relationships. Related: then define classes, attributes, methods; use-case and class diagrams in UML.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is/are feature(s) of inheritance in OOPs?
 Features:
 i) Sub Class
 ii) Super Class
 iii) Reusability
 iv) Operator Overloading
qs.sol:
Concept

Inheritance is the object-oriented mechanism in which a subclass derives attributes or behavior from a superclass. Its main purpose is reuse of existing class definitions; operator overloading is a separate polymorphism feature.

Application

Sub Class: the derived class receives accessible members from another class.

Super Class: the base class supplies members that a derived class can inherit.

Reusability: inherited members let existing implementation be used again instead of being rewritten.

Operator overloading changes how an operator is applied to a user-defined type; it does not define the inheritance relationship. …
qs.rel: Inheritance involves base/derived classes and reusability. Related: operator overloading belongs to polymorphism, not inheritance; access modes (public/protected/private) control derived-class visibility.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about polymorphism in OOPs? 
(i) It may be achieved by function overloading. 
(ii) It is used for reusability.
qs.sol: Statement (i) is true because function overloading represents compile-time polymorphism. Statement (ii) is false as reusability primarily stems from inheritance, not polymorphism itself.
qs.rel: Function overloading is compile-time polymorphism; reusability comes from inheritance. Related: run-time polymorphism uses virtual functions; operator overloading also compile-time.

qs.stem: Which of the following features of object-oriented programming plays an important role in allowing objects having different internal structures to share the same extemal interfaces?
qs.sol:
Polymorphism lets objects of differing internal classes respond through a common external interface.

A common call can invoke class-specific behaviour.
qs.rel: Polymorphism lets differently structured objects share one interface. Related: virtual functions, abstract classes and interfaces; one interface, many implementations.

qs.stem: In which of the following types of inheritance, the properties of a class are inherited by more than one class?
qs.sol:
Hierarchical inheritance has one base class with multiple derived classes.

Each derived class inherits properties from that shared base.
qs.rel: Hierarchical inheritance: one base, many derived classes. Related: multilevel is a chain; multiple has several bases; hybrid combines types; multipath causes the diamond problem.

qs.stem: In C++, trying to access private data from outside of a class throws error. This feature is known as:
qs.sol: In C++, restricting access to class members using private keywords prevents external modification. This mechanism is known as data hiding, which ensures security and integrity of object state.
qs.rel: Making members private blocks outside access: data hiding. Related: abstraction hides implementation; encapsulation bundles; friend functions can bypass hiding.

qs.stem: Which of the following is FALSE with respect to object-in-object Oriented Programming?

Which of the following languages are object-oriented programming languages?

Polymorphism is a fundamental concept in Object Oriented Programming (OOP) that allows objects to take on multiple forms. It enables a single interface to represent different underlying forms (data types). For example, a method can behave differently based on the object that invokes it. This is achieved through features like method overriding and method overloading. Polymorphism is not a feature of procedural, SQL, or non-procedural programming, as these paradigms do not support object-based structures. Therefore, polymorphism is a key feature of Object Oriented Programming. …

Abstraction means focusing on the essential features of an object or concept while ignoring the irrelevant details. It is a fundamental concept in problem-solving and programming, where complex systems are simplified by highlighting key aspects. For example, when designing a car, abstraction allows us to focus on functions like steering and braking without worrying about internal engine mechanics. …

In object-oriented programming (OOP), objects are instances of classes. A class is a blueprint that defines the properties and behaviors of an object. When a class is instantiated, an object is created with its own unique state and behavior.

APPLICATION: When a subclass method calls super().method(), Python searches the MRO after the current class and invokes the inherited implementation through that proxy. The call reuses the existing object; it does not construct an object, define a class, or handle an exception.

qs.stem: In a UML class diagram, a generalization (inheritance) arrow — drawn as a solid line ending in a hollow triangular arrowhead — starts at A and points at B. It means:

opts.A: A is the parent class of B
opts.B: B is the parent class of A
opts.C: A and B are loosely coupled
opts.D: A and B are tightly coupled

qs.sol:
In UML class diagrams, a generalization (inheritance / 'is-a') relationship is drawn as a solid line ending in a hollow, unfilled triangular arrowhead. The arrowhead always attaches to the more general classifier (the superclass/parent), while the plain end attaches to the more specific classifier (the subclass/child): the arrow is read tail to head as child to parent.

Here the arrow starts at A (the tail) and points at B (the head, where the arrowhead sits). Applying the rule above, A is the more specific classifier — the subclass — and B is the more general classifier — the superclass. So the arrow describes B as the parent class of A. …

- **OOP defined:** a paradigm that organises software design around **objects** (data + behaviour) rather than functions and logic. Languages: pure OOP (Smalltalk, Eiffel, Ruby), hybrid (C++, Java, Python, C#). **Simula (1967)** introduced classes/objects. Non-OOP: C, Pascal, FORTRAN, COBOL (original), SQL, LISP (functional, though CLOS adds objects).
- **Class vs object:**

| Class | Object |
|---|---|
| blueprint / template / user-defined type | **instance** of a class |
| no memory for data until instantiated | occupies memory |
| declared once | many objects per class |
| `class Car {...};` | `Car c1, c2;` |

- **Four main concepts** (older books list three: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism; abstraction is the fourth):
  - **Encapsulation** - bundling data and methods into one unit (class) and restricting direct access; protects data (**data hiding**).
  - **Abstraction** - exposing only essential features, hiding implementation (abstract classes, interfaces).
  - **Inheritance** - new class acquires members of an existing class; promotes **reusability**.
  - **Polymorphism** - same operation behaves differently; compile-time (overloading) vs run-time (overriding with virtual functions).
- **Inheritance vocabulary:** base = super = parent class; derived = sub = child class. Types: **single** (one base), **multiple** (several bases; C++ yes, Java classes no), **multilevel** (chain A->B->C), **hierarchical** (one base, many derived; the base's properties are inherited by more than one class), **hybrid/multipath** (combination; can cause the diamond problem, solved in C++ by virtual base classes).
- **Message passing:** objects interact by sending messages, i.e. invoking each other's methods through public interfaces; they need not know each other's internal data or code.
- **Dynamic vs static binding:** static (early, compile time) for overloaded functions and non-virtual calls; dynamic (late, run time) for virtual calls.
- **Procedural vs OOP:**

| Procedural | OOP |
|---|---|
| top-down | **bottom-up** |
| functions are central | objects / data central |
| data global, freely moves between functions | data hidden, accessed via methods |
| little reuse | inheritance and reuse |
| C, Pascal | C++, Java |

- **OOP analysis steps:** first identify the objects and their relationships (**data modelling**), then define classes, attributes, behaviours.
- **Benefits:** modularity, reuse, extensibility, easier maintenance, real-world modelling, security through hiding. **Costs:** more memory/overhead, steeper learning curve.
- **Related terms:** *instantiation* = creating an object; *attribute/data member/field* = data; *method/member function* = behaviour; *constructor/destructor* = lifecycle; *interface* = contract of public operations; *overloading* is not inheritance; *operator overloading* is polymorphism not inheritance.
- **Common traps:** abstraction hides *implementation* (design level), encapsulation hides *data* (implementation level); "function overloading" is polymorphism, not data security; reusability comes from inheritance, not polymorphism; "abduction" is a distractor for "abstraction".
- **Likely question angles:**
  - Which feature secures data (encapsulation) / enables reuse (inheritance) / allows many forms (polymorphism).
  - Name the type of inheritance from a class diagram or description (single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple, hybrid).
  - True/false about OOP being top-down, bottom-up, procedure-centred.
  - Distinguish data hiding vs abstraction vs encapsulation.
  - Which of the listed languages are OOP (Simula, Smalltalk, Java, C++, Ada, Ruby, SQL, LISP).
  - How do objects communicate; what is a message.
  - What is the relation between object and class; what is a user-defined type.
  - Compile-time vs run-time polymorphism example.
  - What problem does virtual base class solve.

topics.title: 6. C++ Classes, Constructors, Inheritance & Polymorphism
topics.theory:
- **Access specifiers:** `private`, `protected`, `public`; default is **private for class** and **public for struct**.
- **Constructor:** same name as class, **no return type**, called automatically at object creation, can be overloaded, can have parameters; kinds: default, parameterised, **copy** (`A(const A&)` - takes a reference), dynamic. Not inherited.
- **Destructor:** `~ClassName()`, **no parameters**, no return type, one per class, called automatically on destruction, can be `virtual`; constructors cannot be virtual.
- **Friend function/class:** not a member, but can access **private and protected** members; a friend class's member functions get that access; friendship is not inherited or mutual.
- **Static member function** accesses only static members and can be called as `Class::f()`. **const member function** (`void f() const`) cannot modify the object.
- **Inheritance modes:** public (public->public, protected->protected), protected (public & protected -> protected), private (all accessible -> private); base **private members are never accessible** to the derived class.
- **Overloading** = same name, different parameters (compile-time; return type alone is not enough); **overriding** = redefine base method in derived class (run-time, needs `virtual`); `Base::f()` calls the base version via the **scope resolution operator**.
- **Virtual function:** member of a base class, redefined in derived classes, accessed through a base pointer/reference for run-time binding.
- **Operator overloading:** member binary operator takes **one** explicit argument (`Matrix operator+(Matrix m)`); `?:`, `::`, `.`, `sizeof` cannot be overloaded.
- **Exceptions:** `try/catch/throw`; synchronous (array index out of range) vs asynchronous (keyboard interrupt). Constructor parameters that shadow members only change the local copy.

qs.stem: Which of the following type of constructors (in C++) does NOT accept parameters?
qs.sol: A default constructor in C++ is defined as a constructor that can be called without any arguments. While parameterized constructors require specific input values and copy constructors take an object reference, the default constructor initializes objects without external parameters.
qs.rel: A default constructor can be called with no arguments (compiler supplies one only if none is declared). Related: parameterised constructor takes arguments; copy constructor takes a const reference; constructors have no return type.

qs.stem: In C++, which of the following defines how the members (attributes and methods) of a class can be accessed?
qs.sol:
Class members can be declared public, protected or private.

These access specifiers control where attributes and methods are accessible.
qs.rel: Access specifiers private, protected, public control member visibility. Related: class defaults to private, struct to public; protected is visible to derived classes; friend bypasses restrictions.

qs.stem: Which of the following is used to access the overridden function of the base class from the derived class?
qs.sol: The scope resolution operator :: accesses overridden base class functions from a derived class. This syntax explicitly calls the parent implementation instead of the overridden version.
qs.rel: The scope resolution operator :: calls a base-class version explicitly, e.g. Base::show(). Related: :: also accesses globals and namespace members; overriding redefines base methods; virtual gives run-time dispatch.

qs.stem: Which of the following type of constructors is used to initialise data members with the values provided by the user in C++?
qs.sol: A parameterised constructor accepts arguments when an object is created. Those arguments initialise its data members.
qs.rel: A parameterised constructor initialises members with the supplied arguments. Related: constructors can be overloaded; initialisation lists; a default constructor is not auto-generated once any constructor is defined.

qs.stem: Which of the following functions should be the destructor function for user defined class Person in C++?
qs.sol: In C++, a destructor must be named with the class name preceded by a tilde symbol and cannot accept parameters. Option 3 correctly defines ~Person() which strictly adheres to this specific syntax requirement for user-defined classes.
qs.rel: Destructor is ~ClassName() with no parameters and no return type. Related: one per class; called automatically in reverse order of construction; may be virtual; cannot be overloaded.

qs.stem: By default in C++, the member of a class are _____, while, by default the member of structure are _____.
qs.rel: C++ class members default private; struct members default public. Related: union members public; inheritance default is private for class, public for struct.

qs.stem: In C++, if a function f is defined as a friend function, then which of the following category of data members can be accessed using the function f ?
qs.sol: In C++, a friend function is declared outside the class but granted special access privileges. It can access all data members of the class, including private, protected, and public categories.
qs.rel: A friend function can access private, protected and public members of the class. Related: friend is not a member and not inherited; friendship is not mutual; friend classes allowed.

qs.stem: A ________ function is a member function in base class that you expect to redefine in derived classes.
qs.sol: A virtual function is declared in a base class using the virtual keyword to enable polymorphism. This allows derived classes to override the function, ensuring the correct implementation is called at runtime based on the object type.
qs.rel: Virtual functions are declared in the base class for run-time overriding. Related: pure virtual (=0) makes an abstract class; needs pointer/reference for dynamic dispatch; virtual destructor.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements with reference to constructors in Object Oriented Programming is FALSE?

opts.B: Constructor is a special function that helps you instantiate an object of a class.
opts.C: Whenever you instantiate an object, a default constructor method is called.
opts.D: Default constructors do not take any parameters.

qs.sol: A constructor initializes an object and does not return a value, so the printed key selects the statement that constructors return a value. The question is ambiguous: the claim that a default constructor is called whenever an object is instantiated is also too broad, because arguments can invoke a matching parameterized constructor.
qs.rel: Constructors return no value (not even void). Related: they initialise objects, may be overloaded, can have parameters, are called automatically at object creation.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements with reference to constructor in C++ is FALSE?

opts.A: It should not have the same name as the class.
opts.B: It is a special method that is automatically called when an object of a class is created.
opts.D: It does not have any return value.

qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: 'It is always public' was changed to 'It can be public' because C++ permits private and protected constructors. A constructor must have the same name as its class, making the official keyed claim the sole false statement.
qs.rel: Constructors must have the same name as the class. Related: automatically called at creation; can be public, protected or private (singleton pattern); no return type.

qs.stem: Which of the following is FALSE with respect to constructors in C++?

opts.B: Constructors are used to initialise variables and to allocate memory
opts.C: When an object is created and initialised, at the same time, a copy constructor gets called
opts.D: A constructor should not have the same name as that of a class

qs.sol:
In C++, a constructor has the same name as its class and has no return type.

Therefore the assertion that the names should differ is false.
qs.rel: A constructor has the same name as its class (so 'should differ' is false) and no return type. Related: constructors can be overloaded, initialise members, and allocate resources.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements with reference to constructor and destructor in C++ is FALSE?

opts.A: The destructor can have parameters, but the constructor does not receive any parameters.
opts.B: A constructor is called by the compiler whenever the object of the class is created.
opts.C: A destructor is called by the compiler when the object is destroyed.
opts.D: Both constructor and destructor can be defined as public, private, or protected.

qs.sol: In C++, constructors may accept parameters, while destructors cannot. The statement reverses those rules and is therefore false.
qs.rel: Constructors can take parameters; destructors cannot. Related: destructor name ~Class, never overloaded, called automatically; constructors can be overloaded.

qs.stem: Which of the following, associated with a friend class, can directly access private and protected data?
qs.sol:
Friendship grants the member functions of the declared friend class access to the granting class’s private and protected members.

This privilege does not automatically extend to arbitrary classes or free functions.
qs.rel: Friend class member functions can access private and protected members of the granting class. Related: friendship is not inherited and not symmetric; use sparingly.

qs.stem: Which of the following is the process of initialising an object from another object using a copy constructor in C++?
qs.sol:
Initialising a new object from an existing object with a copy constructor is copy initialisation in the wording of this paper.

The constructor carries out the copying during that initialisation.
qs.rel: Initialising a new object from another via the copy constructor is copy initialisation. Related: A b = a; or A b(a); pass-by-value triggers it; assignment operator is different.

qs.stem: In C++, “Out-of-range-index” belong to _____ type exception while keyboard interrupts are called _____ exceptions.
qs.sol:
In C++ exception handling:

“Out-of-range-index” exceptions occur during program execution due to program logic or invalid indexing. These are synchronous exceptions because they occur as a direct result of program instructions.

Keyboard interrupts occur due to external events independent of the program flow. These are asynchronous exceptions.

Therefore, the correct answer is synchronous; asynchronous.
qs.rel: Out-of-range index is a synchronous exception; keyboard interrupt is asynchronous. Related: C++ exceptions handle synchronous ones; try-catch-throw; signals handle asynchronous.

qs.stem: Which of the following can be the declaration of a member function if it does NOT alter any data in the class?
qs.sol:
Declaring a member function const promises that it will not modify the observable state of its object through this.

The const qualifier is written after the function parameter list.
qs.rel: A const member function (void f() const) promises not to change the object. Related: const objects can call only const functions; mutable overrides for particular members.

qs.stem: In case of protected inheritance in C++, which of the following correctly represents the accessibility of the data variables from second derived class?

opts.A: Private variables: Yes, Protected variables: Yes, Public variables: Yes
opts.B: Private variables: Yes, Protected variables: No, Public variables: Yes
opts.C: Private variables: No, Protected variables: Yes, Public variables: Yes
opts.D: Private variables: No, Protected variables: No, Public variables: Yes

qs.sol: In protected inheritance, base class private members remain inaccessible to all derived classes. Public and protected members of the base class become protected in the first derived class, allowing access from a second derived class within its scope. Therefore, private variables are inaccessible while protected and public base variables are accessible as protected.
qs.rel: Protected inheritance makes base public and protected members protected, so second-level derived classes can still reach them. Related: base private never accessible; public inheritance keeps modes.

qs.stem:
Which of the following options best describes the truthfulness of the given statements with reference to destructors?

(i) Destructors are the last member function called for an object and they are called by the compiler itself.

(ii) A destructor can be declared in any section of the class.
qs.sol: A destructor runs as an object is destroyed and can be declared in any access section of a C++ class. Both stated propositions are true.
qs.rel: Destructors are called by the compiler as the object ends and can be in any access section. Related: private destructor prevents stack objects; virtual destructor in base classes.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about copy constructor in C++?

opts.A: It is the constructor that does not accept parameters.
opts.B: It is member function of a class.
opts.C: It is used to initialise the object by another object.
opts.D: It accepts objects of the same class as a reference.

qs.sol: A copy constructor initializes a new object from an existing one of the same class type. It requires a reference parameter to access that source object data. Consequently, stating it accepts no parameters is false, making Option A the correct selection.
qs.rel: Copy constructor takes a reference to an object of same class, so 'accepts no parameters' is wrong. Related: A(const A&); shallow vs deep copy; invoked on pass-by-value.

qs.stem: In case of public inheritance in C++, which of the following correctly represents the accessibility of the data variables from derived class?

opts.A: Private variables: Yes, Protected variables: Yes, Public variables: Yes
opts.B: Private variables: Yes, Protected variables: No, Public variables: Yes
opts.C: Private variables: No, Protected variables: Yes, Public variables: Yes
opts.D: Private variables: No, Protected variables: No, Public variables: Yes

qs.sol: In C++ public inheritance, private members of the base class remain inaccessible to the derived class. Protected and public members are accessible within the derived class, though their accessibility levels may change relative to external code.
qs.rel: Public inheritance: base public and protected stay accessible; private stays inaccessible. Related: protected becomes visible to the derived class but not outside it.

qs.stem:
Select true or FALSE from the below sentences.

(i) a private member function can only be called by another function that is a member of its class

(ii) an object can invoke a private function using the dot operator
qs.sol:
A private member function is callable from another member of its class.

An object cannot call it directly through the dot operator because private access is enforced.
qs.rel: A private member function can be called only by class members/friends; objects cannot call it via dot. Related: same applies to private data; helper functions are kept private.

qs.stem: In case of private inheritance in C++, which of the following correctly represents the accessibility of the data variables from second derived class?

opts.A: Private variables: Yes, Protected variables: No, Public variables: Yes
opts.B: Private variables: Yes, Protected variables: No, Public variables: No
opts.C: Private variables: Yes, Protected variables: Yes, Public variables: Yes
opts.D: Private variables: No, Protected variables: No, Public variables: No

qs.sol:
Concept: Inheritance determines how a derived class can access members of its base; it does not change where those members are declared. Private inheritance makes the base’s public and protected members accessible as private through the immediate derived class.

A base’s private members require permission from that base, such as friendship. Further derivation does not itself grant access to members accessible only as private through the intermediate class.

Application: Use ordinary inherited-member access in a two-level hierarchy, without friends, using declarations that expose members, or accessor functions. …
qs.rel: Private inheritance makes all accessible base members private in the derived class, so a further derived class sees nothing. Related: default for class; 'implemented in terms of'.

qs.stem:
Which statement is correct about static member function in C++?
 I. It can access only other static members declared in the same class.
 II. It cannot be called using the class name (instead of its objects).
qs.sol:
In C++, a static member function belongs to the class rather than to any specific object.

Statement I:
A static member function can directly access only static data members and other static member functions of the same class.
So, Statement I is correct.

Statement II:
Static member functions can be called using the class name without creating objects.
Example:

ClassName::functionName();

Therefore, Statement II is incorrect.

Hence, the correct answer is Only I.
qs.rel: A static member function touches only static members and may be called with Class::f(). Related: has no this pointer; cannot be virtual or const.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is NOT correct about virtual functions in C++?

I. A virtual function must be a member of a class.

II. It can be accessed using an object pointer or reference.
qs.sol:
Key idea

A virtual function in C++ is a member function declared with the virtual keyword, usually in a base class.

Statement check

Statement I: Correct. A non-member or global function cannot be declared virtual.

Statement II: Correct. Dynamic binding is commonly achieved by calling the virtual function through a base-class pointer or reference.

Conclusion

Both statements are correct, so no listed statement is “NOT correct.”

Final answer: Neither I nor II.
qs.rel: A virtual function must be a class member and is invoked through base pointers/references for dynamic binding. Related: cannot be static or a constructor; destructors may be virtual.

qs.stem:
Match the following.

(i)

	

Overriding

	

1

	

Allows a function or operator to be given more than one definition
qs.sol:
Overriding changes an inherited method definition, matching 3.

Overloading permits more than one function or operator definition, matching 1.

A destructor deallocates resources, matching 2.

head: (ii)
Over loading
rows: A function that is called to deallocate memory
The ability to change the definition of an inherited method

qs.rel: Overriding redefines an inherited method; overloading gives several definitions; destructor deallocates memory. Related: constructor allocates/initialises; virtual enables dynamic overriding.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements with reference to function overloading in C++ is FALSE?

opts.A: Function overloading can also be treated as compile-time polymorphism.
opts.B: You can overload function declarations that differ only by return type.
opts.C: The process of selecting the most appropriate overloaded function or operator is called overload resolution.
opts.D: There should be a difference in the number or kind of parameters.

qs.sol:
C++ selects an overload from its function name and parameter list.

Return type alone cannot distinguish two overload declarations.
qs.rel: Overloads must differ in parameter list, not return type alone. Related: compile-time polymorphism; name mangling; default arguments can cause ambiguity.

qs.sol:
The overloaded arrow operator returns this, so ob->a and ob.a refer to the same member.

Assignment stores 10, and both expressions print that value.

The printed Hindi code omits -> in the operator declaration; as printed, that version is invalid C++. The official 10 10 answer follows the English code.
qs.rel: Overloaded -> returning this makes ob->a same as ob.a; prints 10. Related: operator-> must return a pointer or object; smart pointers use it.

qs.stem:
Identify the correct statements. 
(i) Derived classes do not inherit or overload constructors or destructors from their base classes. 
(ii) Destructors can be declared with the keyword virtual. 
(iii) Constructors can be declared with the keyword virtual.
qs.sol: In C++, constructors and destructors are not inherited members, confirming statement (i). Destructors can be declared virtual to ensure proper resource cleanup during polymorphic deletion, supporting statement (ii). Conversely, constructors cannot be virtual, making statement (iii) incorrect. Thus, the valid statements are only (i) and (ii).
qs.rel: Constructors/destructors are not inherited; destructors may be virtual; constructors cannot be. Related: base constructor runs first; virtual destructors prevent leaks via base pointers.

qs.sol: Creating wall1 calls Wall() automatically. The constructor prints its first message, then the length value 5.5 on the next line.
qs.rel: Constructor runs automatically at object creation, printing messages and setting length = 5.5. Related: constructor/destructor print order; default constructor.

qs.stem:
In C++, the "+" operator is overloaded (as member operator function) in user defined class Matrix that adds two matrices and returns resultant matrix. 

Which of the following is a signature of this operator function?
qs.sol: For a binary operator overloaded as a member function, the left operand is the object that calls the function and the right operand is the single explicit parameter. So A + B is internally treated as A.operator+(B). The function must return a Matrix because adding two matrices gives another Matrix. Therefore, the correct signature is Matrix operator+(Matrix B). Hence, Option B is correct.
qs.rel: Binary operator overloaded as a member takes one argument: Matrix operator+(Matrix m) (left operand is *this). Related: friend version takes two; unary has none.

qs.sol:
In C++, a constructor parameter that shares its name with a data member shadows that member inside the constructor's body — assigning to it changes only the local parameter, never the object's member, unless it is written explicitly via the this pointer (this->a = a). In-class default member initializers (like int a=10, b=20;) run once, before the constructor body executes, and apply only to the object actually being constructed; a separate local object created inside that body owns its own independent copy of the members.

int main(){ A y; } calls A's default constructor A() on object y.

Before A()'s body runs, y's own members are set by the default initializers: a = 10, b = 20. …
qs.rel: A constructor parameter named like a member shadows it; the assignment changes only the local copy. Related: this->a = a; private default in class; compile errors for private constructors.

qs.stem: In C++, which of the following is not a valid access specifier?
qs.sol: Class access levels control member visibility. The remaining word is a qualifier permitting a data member to change even through a const object.

qs.stem: Which of the following feature is not supported in C++ ?
qs.sol:
Concept

Object-oriented language features describe different ways to organize types and choose behavior. Inheritance derives one class from another, abstraction exposes an interface while hiding details, and dynamic binding selects an overridden virtual function at run time. Reflection instead inspects a program’s own types or members as metadata.

Application

For the 2019 exam’s C++ context, classes can inherit, abstract interfaces can be written, and virtual functions provide dynamic dispatch. General language-level reflection of arbitrary class structure was not part of that C++ standard; limited compile-time type traits are a different facility. …

C++ is a programming language developed as an extension of C. It was created to add object-oriented features while maintaining compatibility with C.

The original creator of C++ is a single individual who worked on extending C with new features like classes, inheritance, and polymorphism.

To determine the correct option, evaluate each name based on their known contributions to programming languages.

Dennis Ritchie and Brian Kernighan are known for creating the C language, not C++. Ken Thompson is known for Unix and early C development, not C++.

Bjarne Stroustrup is the individual who developed C++ at Bell Labs, starting in the early 1980s. …

qs.stem: Which of the following is the scope resolution operator in C++ language ?
qs.sol: C++ uses a pair of colons to qualify names by namespace or class scope. The other symbols represent member access, pointer operations, or bitwise complement/destructor syntax.

qs.stem: Which of the following is the original creator of the C++ language?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
C++ was designed and initially implemented by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs.

The other named people are associated with C or Unix rather than creation of C++.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not a type of constructor?
qs.sol: Constructors are special member functions that are invoked automatically when an object of a class is created. They have the same name as the class and do not have a return type. A Friend Function is a function that is not a member of a class but has permission to access its private and protected members. Because a constructor must be a member of the class it belongs to, a "Friend Constructor" is a logical contradiction in C++ syntax.

qs.stem: How many types of polymorphisms are supported by C++?
qs.sol:
C++ supports two main types of polymorphism:

1. Compile-time (static) polymorphism: The function or operation to be executed is decided during compilation. Examples include function overloading, operator overloading, and templates.

2. Run-time (dynamic) polymorphism: The function to be executed is decided during program execution. This is achieved using inheritance and virtual functions.

Therefore, the correct answer is 2.

qs.stem: Which concept of C++ is used to reuse the written code?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: In C++, the concept used to reuse written code is inheritance. Inheritance allows a class to inherit properties and methods from another class, enabling the reuse of existing code without rewriting it. This promotes code efficiency and reduces redundancy.

qs.stem: What is the purpose of a destructor in OOP?

opts.C: To free up resources when an object is destroyed
opts.D: To define default values for properties

qs.stem: Inheritance allows the following in C++ program :
qs.sol: Inheritance lets a derived class reuse members of a base class, establishes a class hierarchy, and allows behavior to be extended. Each listed benefit therefore applies.

qs.stem: In C++, all members of a class are _____ by default.

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
C++ gives class members a default access level when no specifier is written.

That default is private, unlike the default for a struct.

qs.stem: In C++, all members of a class are _____ by default.
qs.sol:
Concept

An architectural pattern separates software responsibilities so that each part has a defined concern. Model–View–Controller is the pattern whose three roles are the model, the view, and the controller.

The model manages application data and domain logic, the view presents information, and the controller interprets input and coordinates updates between the other roles.

Application

The question asks for the architecture named by exactly those three components. Their initials form MVC, so MVC is the matching architecture.

Contrast

Client-server classifies communicating participants as clients and servers. …

qs.stem: In C++, which of the following operator cannot be overloaded?
qs.sol: C++ permits overloads for bitwise XOR (^), equality (==), and logical NOT (!). The direct member-access operator . cannot be overloaded.

qs.stem: A constructor is called whenever

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: A constructor is a special member function that is invoked when an object is created. It initializes the newly created object, so the correct option is an object is created.

qs.stem: A generic function can be created using the following :
qs.sol: A C++ function template describes an algorithm with type parameters. The compiler instantiates it for particular types, creating a generic function interface.

opts.C: It handles unexpected errors and allows graceful program termination
opts.D: It eliminates the need for classes and objects

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

A C++ class groups data members and member functions in one type.

Data alone is only part of the class, and the combined data-and-functions description is also correct.

qs.stem: In C++, what does a class hold?
qs.sol:
Concept

In Java Swing, interactive components expose semantic events through the event-listener model. A source component fires an event object, and a registered listener receives it and runs the associated command.

A push-button click is represented by ActionEvent, which is delivered to ActionListener implementations registered with that button.

Application

JButton is the Swing push-button component. Clicking a JButton changes its ButtonModel state and causes the button to fire an ActionEvent to its registered ActionListener instances.

Contrast

JLabel presents non-editable text or an icon rather than acting as a push-button control. …

qs.stem: Which of the following constructors is provided by the C++ compiler if not defined in a class?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
When a class declares no constructors, C++ implicitly declares a default constructor so an object can be default-initialized.

A parameterized constructor is never supplied merely because the programmer omitted one. The official key selects the default-constructor description.

Note: An eligible copy constructor can also be implicitly declared, so the printed question is ambiguous if it asks for every compiler-provided constructor.

qs.stem: Which of the following constructors is provided by the C++ compiler if not defined in a class?

In a bottom-up parser, a reduce move replaces the right-hand side of a production by its left-hand side non-terminal.

Here, productions of the form A → ε and A → a are not allowed. Therefore, every reduction must replace at least two stack symbols by one non-terminal. Each reduce move decreases the number of stack symbols by at least 1.

Initially, there are n input tokens on the stack. Finally, the parse must leave one start symbol. So the number of reductions can be at most n − 1. This maximum is achieved when every reduction combines exactly two symbols into one.

Hence, the maximum number of reduce moves is n − 1.

topics.deep:
- **Class syntax:** `class Wall { private: double length; public: Wall(){length=5.5; cout<<"Creating a wall.";} };` Creating `Wall w;` automatically calls the constructor. Defaults: **class -> private**, **struct -> public**, union -> public.
- **Access specifiers:**

| Specifier | Same class | Derived class | Outside |
|---|---|---|---|
| private | yes | no | no |
| protected | yes | yes | no |
| public | yes | yes | yes |

  Friend functions/classes bypass this. Trying to access private data from outside is a compile error (**data hiding**).
- **Inheritance modes (members of base -> in derived):** public inheritance: public->public, protected->protected; protected inheritance: public->protected, protected->protected; private inheritance: public->private, protected->private. Base **private** members are *never* directly accessible. For a second derived class: after private inheritance nothing from the original base is accessible; after protected inheritance protected/public are still accessible (as protected). Syntax `class D : public B {}`. Constructors run base-first, destructors derived-first.
- **Constructors:** same name as class; no return type (not even void); automatically invoked; can be overloaded; public, private or protected; not inherited, cannot be virtual; initialisation list `A(int x):a(x){}`.

| Kind | Form | Use |
|---|---|---|
| default | `A()` | callable with no arguments |
| parameterised | `A(int)` | initialise with user-supplied values |
| copy | `A(const A&)` | build from another object (copy initialisation) |
| dynamic | uses `new` inside | allocate memory at creation |

  Copy constructor takes a **reference** (otherwise infinite recursion); invoked on `A b = a;`, pass-by-value, return-by-value.
- **Destructor:** `~A()`, no args, no return, one per class, may be `virtual`, may be in any access section, called when object goes out of scope/`delete`; compiler calls it. Shadowing trap: `A(int a,int b){a=30;b=40;}` assigns the *parameters*, members remain 10 and 20 unless `this->a` is used.
- **Friend:** `friend void f(A&);` / `friend class B;` - can access private and protected members; not inherited, not mutual, not a member.
- **Special members:** `static` member shared by all objects; `static` member function only touches static data, callable as `A::f()`; `const` member function `int get() const` cannot change data; `this` pointer; inline functions.
- **Polymorphism:**
  - *Overloading*: same name, different parameter list (number/type/order); return type alone cannot differ. Compile time.
  - *Overriding*: same signature in derived class; use **virtual** in base for run-time dispatch; call base version with `Base::f()`.
  - *Virtual function*: member declared with `virtual`, accessed via pointer/reference; must be a class member; pure virtual `= 0` makes class abstract.
- **Operator overloading:** `Matrix operator+(const Matrix &m)` as member - **one** parameter for binary operator (left operand is `*this`); friend version needs two. Not overloadable: `::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:`, `sizeof`. Overloaded `->` must return a pointer/object with `->`: `example* operator->(){return this;}`.
- **Exceptions:** `try { throw x; } catch(type e){}`; **synchronous** exceptions come from the program logic (array index out of range, divide by zero); **asynchronous** from outside events (keyboard interrupt, hardware failure) - C++ handles only synchronous ones.
- **Common traps:** `class` default private vs `struct` public; copy constructor parameter by value is illegal; return type of constructor "void" is wrong; virtual constructor illegal, virtual destructor useful; function with only return type difference is not overload.
- **Likely question angles:**
  - Which members does a derived class see for public/protected/private inheritance.
  - Output of a small program with constructor/destructor print statements (order of calls for two objects and for derived classes).
  - Identify the false statement about constructors/destructors/friend/static.
  - Signature of an overloaded `==`, `<<` or `++` operator.
  - What is printed when a virtual vs non-virtual function is called through a base pointer.
  - Function overloading ambiguity: `f(int)` and `f(double)` called with `f('a')` or `f(3.5f)`.
  - Valid/invalid constructor declarations.
  - Difference between shallow and deep copy.
  - Why is a copy constructor needed for a class with a pointer member.

topics.title: 7. Java Fundamentals & Features
topics.theory:
- **Java compiler (`javac`) produces bytecode** (`.class`), run by the **JVM**; `javap` **disassembles** class files; the `PATH` variable locates `javac`/`java`.
- **All code lives in classes**; member functions are called **methods**; defining a method outside the class or putting `;` after a method header is wrong.
- **Inheritance:** `class B extends A` (single class inheritance only); `implements` for interfaces - a class can implement **multiple interfaces**.
- **`final`:** final class cannot be inherited, final method cannot be overridden, final variable is a constant.
- **Overloading** is resolved at **compile time** by parameter types; **overriding** is resolved at **run time** by the object's actual type.
- **Wrapper classes:** `Integer` for `int`; primitives are lowercase (`int, byte, short, long, float, double, char, boolean`).
- **Operators:** relational `<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=` (`=>` is invalid); string `+` concatenates left to right (`"exam:"+9+9+9` = `exam:999`); `<<` on `byte` is done in `int` then cast.
- **Constructors:** `this(...)` calls another constructor and must be the **first statement**; no-arg constructor is provided only if none is written.
- **Exceptions:** `try/catch/finally`; `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` for bad index; `catch(Exception e)` prints `java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3`.
- **Upcasting/downcasting:** `Object o = new String("x"); String s = (String) o;` is valid at run time.
- **Identifiers** may contain letters, digits, `_`, `$`; keywords like `static` are reserved. Java web services: SOAP and RESTful.

qs.stem: JAVA compiler translates source code into __________.
qs.sol:
Unlike many other languages that compile directly into machine-specific code, Java uses a two-step process to ensure portability across different operating systems.

Source Code to Bytecode: The Java compiler (javac) takes your human-readable .java files and translates them into Bytecode (stored in .class files).

Platform Independence: This bytecode is not specific to any particular processor. Instead, it is designed to be executed by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).

Execution: The JVM then translates the bytecode into the actual machine code of the specific device you are using (Windows, Mac, Linux, etc.).
qs.rel: javac produces platform-independent bytecode (.class) run by the JVM; JIT compiles hot bytecode to native code. Related: javap disassembles class files, java launches the JVM, bytecode is not machine code.

qs.stem: What is garbage collection in the context of Java?

opts.A: The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) checks the output of any Java program and deletes anything that does not make sense at all.
opts.B: The Operating System periodically deletes all of the Java files available on the system.

qs.sol:
In Java, garbage collection is the process of automatically freeing memory used by objects that are no longer needed.

An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when there are no live references to it from any part of the running program.

The JVM reclaims the heap memory used by such unreachable objects automatically.

Key additional points:
 GC timing is non-deterministic: you know an object is eligible for collection, but you cannot predict exactly when the JVM will run the collector.

Calling System.gc() only requests a collection; the JVM may ignore it.

topics.deep:
- **Platform:** Java source `.java` -> `javac` -> **bytecode** `.class` -> **JVM** (interpreter + JIT) -> runs on any OS ("write once, run anywhere"). Tools: `javac` (compiler), `java` (launcher), `javap` (**disassembler**), `javadoc`, `jar`. The `PATH` environment variable lets the OS find `javac`/`java`; `CLASSPATH` finds classes. JDK = JRE + tools; JRE = JVM + libraries.
- **Features:** simple, object-oriented, platform independent, secure, robust (exception handling, garbage collection), multithreaded, distributed, no explicit pointers, **no multiple inheritance of classes** (interfaces instead), no operator overloading, no goto.
- **Program shape:** every function is a member of a class and is called a **method**; `public static void main(String[] args)`. Method headers have **no semicolon**; methods are defined *inside* the braces of a class.
- **Primitive types:**

| Type | Size | Range / note |
|---|---|---|
| byte | 8 bit | -128..127 |
| short | 16 | -32768..32767 |
| int | 32 | about +-2.1e9 |
| long | 64 | |
| float / double | 32 / 64 | |
| char | 16 (Unicode) | |
| boolean | 1 bit logical | true/false only |

  **Wrapper classes:** `Integer, Byte, Short, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean`.
- **Declarations:** `int x = 10;` valid; identifiers can include `_` and `$`, cannot be keywords (`static`, `class`, `final` ...). Relational operators: `< <= > >= == !=`; `=>` invalid. `>>>` unsigned shift.
- **Strings:** `"exam:" + 9 + 9 + 9` -> `exam:999` (left to right); `9 + 9 + "x"` -> `18x`; strings are immutable; `==` compares references, `equals()` compares content.
- **Byte shift trap:** `byte x = 64; byte y = (byte)(x << 4);` 64<<4 = 1024 as int; cast keeps the low 8 bits -> **0**. `byte b = (byte)130;` -> -126.
- **Inheritance/OOP keywords:** `extends` (class from class; also interface from interface), `implements` (class from interfaces; many allowed), `super`, `this`, `abstract`, `interface`, `final`, `static`, `new`, `instanceof`. A class has only **one** superclass; implementing multiple interfaces gives multiple "contract" inheritance.
- **`final`:** class -> cannot be subclassed; method -> cannot be overridden; variable -> assigned once.
- **Overloading vs overriding:** overload resolved at **compile time** on parameter types (static binding); override resolved at **run time** on the object's actual class (dynamic dispatch). Overriding needs same signature, return-compatible type, equal or wider access.
- **Constructors:** same name as class, no return type; if none written the compiler adds a default; `this(10)` as the *first* statement chains constructors. Example: `Test(){ this(10); System.out.println("no-arg"); } Test(int x){System.out.println("param "+x);}` output: `param 10` then `no-arg`.
- **Access modifiers:**

| Modifier | Class | Package | Subclass | World |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| private | Y | N | N | N |
| default | Y | Y | N | N |
| protected | Y | Y | Y | N |
| public | Y | Y | Y | Y |

- **Exceptions:** hierarchy `Throwable -> Error / Exception -> RuntimeException`; checked vs unchecked; keywords `try catch finally throw throws`. `int[] n={1,2,3}; n[5]` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3`; `finally` always runs. Packages group classes (`import java.util.*;`).
- **Casting:** `Object o = new String("hi"); String s = (String) o;` is fine; `(Integer) o` fails with `ClassCastException`.
- **Loops/pre-increment trap:** `int m=1000,k=3000; while(++m < --k);` stops when m meets k: m = 2000.
- **Likely question angles:**
  - Output of string-concatenation puzzles (`1 + 2 + "a" + 3`).
  - What the compiler produces / what `javap` does / which variable locates `javac`.
  - Valid vs invalid Java identifiers, keywords (`goto` reserved, `const` reserved).
  - Output of try/catch/finally program (order of prints).
  - Which statement about `final`, `static`, `abstract`, interfaces is true.
  - Method overloading vs overriding in a given code (which method runs).
  - Wrapper class for `char` / `boolean` / `double`.
  - Result of integer overflow or byte casting.
  - Can a class extend two classes? Implement two interfaces?

topics.title: 8. Visual Basic, VBScript & .NET
topics.theory:
- **Visual Basic** released by Microsoft in **1991**; **VB 6.0 (1998)** was the last classic version before **VB.NET**; IDE = **Integrated Development Environment**; project file extension **.vbp**.
- **Data types (VB6):** Byte 1, Integer 2, **Long 4** (-2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647), Single 4, Double 8, **Currency 8**, Date 8, Boolean 2, String, Variant. **Date and String are non-numeric.**
- **Type suffixes:** `%` Integer, `&` Long, `!` Single, `#` Double, `@` Currency, `$` String.
- **Operators:** `/` division, **`\` integer division**, `Mod`, `&` concatenation, `^` power. **Functions:** `Len("Visual Basic Tutorial")` = 21; `InStr(1,"Visual Basic","Basic")` = 8.
- **Loops:** `For...Next`, `Do...Loop`, `While...Wend`; there is no `Repeat...Until`.
- **Controls:** TextBox (input + output), Label (output only), CheckBox (multiple choices), **OptionButton/RadioButton (one of many, e.g. gender)**, CommandButton, ComboBox, PictureBox, Image, Line, Shape. Control naming prefixes `txt, btn/cmd, lbl`; names cannot contain spaces or `+`.
- **Graphics methods:** `PSet` (point), `Line`, `Circle`. **Name** is a property common to all controls; `Form.StartPosition` sets the initial form position; `Dock` positions a ToolStrip.
- **Events:** menu item code goes in the **Click** event; handler form `cmdOK_Click(sender, e)`; **Index** property = position in a control array.
- **Debugging:** **F10 = Step Over**, F8 = Step Into (VB6), **Break All** pauses execution; windows: Immediate (values), Properties, Project Explorer, Toolbox.
- **Parameters:** default passing is **ByRef** (VB6); `ByVal` passes a copy. Scope: procedure, module/form, global.
- **VBScript:** default scripting language of **ASP**; `Option Explicit` forces declarations; variables declared by `Dim`, `Public`, `Private` (not `Protected`); `<script language="VBScript">`; single type **Variant** with subtypes (Empty, Null, Currency, Error...).
- **.NET:** languages C#, F#, J#, VB.NET compile to **IL** run by the **CLR**; Pascal is non-.NET. VB works with Access, Oracle, MySQL through ADO/ODBC/DAO.

Should begin with a letter

Cannot contain special symbols like +

Spaces

The + symbol

qs.stem: What does the Form.StartPosition property represent in Visual Basic?

opts.A: It determine the end position of the form
opts.B: It determines the initial position of the form
opts.C: It determines the current position of the form
opts.D: It determines the next position of the form

qs.sol:
In Visual Basic, the Form.StartPosition property is used to specify the starting location of a form when it appears on the screen.

This property determines where the form will be displayed initially, such as:

CenterScreen → form appears at the center of the screen

Manual → programmer sets the position manually

WindowsDefaultLocation → Windows decides the position

Statement B is correct because StartPosition controls the initial position of the form.

The other options are incorrect because this property is not related to the end position, current position, or next position of the form.
qs.rel: StartPosition sets the initial location of a form (CenterScreen, Manual, WindowsDefaultLocation). Related: Location, Size, WindowState, FormBorderStyle are other form properties.

Application

Substitute the intermediate values and evaluate from left to right: 4 + 8 - 10 = 12 - 10 = 2.

Cross-check: Adding 10 back to the result gives 12, equal to the remainder 4 plus the product 8. Thus the output is 2.

qs.stem:
How many times the below FOR LOOP gets executed ?

<SCRIPT LANGUAGE = "VBScript">
    Q = 29
    FOR AGE = 5 to Q STEP 6
    DOCUMENT.WRITE P
    NEXT
</SCRIPT>
A

4 times

B

5 times

C

It will not execute as STEP parameter is wrong

D

It will not execute as P is not enclosed in ( )
qs.sol:
Concept: In a For...Next loop with a positive STEP, the counter starts at the given value, increases by STEP after each repetition, and repeats while it is at or below the end value.

The count therefore includes both endpoints when repeated increments land exactly on the end value.

Set the start to 5, the end to Q = 29, and the increment to 6.

The counter values at the start of successive repetitions are 5, 11, 17, 23, and 29; all satisfy AGE ≤ 29.

After the repetition at 29, adding 6 gives 35. Since 35 > 29, the loop stops before a sixth repetition.

Cross-check: (29 − 5) ÷ 6 + 1 = 5. The loop therefore executes 5 times. …
